items.title: Meta, Google Invest in Long-Duration Batteries to Power AI
body: Soaring energy demand for artificial intelligence has spurred billions of dollars in clean energy investments, such as in next-generation geothermal and advanced nuclear reactors. Now, hyperscalers are boosting yet another clean technology: long-lasting batteries.

Developers are starting to add these batteries, known as long-duration energy storage, to data centers. As they do that, there’s a real chance to scale them and unlock more renewable energy, experts say.

“Long-duration storage is an important addition to a growing toolkit that can help us build AI infrastructure at unprecedented scale,” said Cully Cavness, cofounder and president at Crusoe, which builds and operates AI data centers for tech giants.

Long-duration energy storage is an umbrella term for technologies capable of storing and releasing electricity for many hours or even days. Conventional lithium-ion batteries, in contrast, only hold power for a few hours.

The idea of creating super batteries has been around for years, but they have been slow to take off because they are expensive and remain unproven at scale. That is poised to change with a rapidly expanding pipeline.

Since the beginning of 2025, at least 150 gigawatt-hours’ worth of new long-duration storage projects have either been announced, permitted or secured financing in the US, according to an estimate by BloombergNEF. That represents more than a fivefold increase from the country’s total planned installations as of late 2024, BNEF data shows, with the majority of the new demand coming from AI data centers.

The influx of capital from AI data center operators is not just expanding the scale of deployment; it is also opening the door for a wide range of technologies. In Arizona, Alphabet Inc.’s Google is working with Energy Dome, an Italian company, to store power for 10 hours in batteries made of carbon dioxide, while Crusoe has teamed up with California-based Energy Vault to harness gravity as a storage tool.

Meta Platforms Inc., meanwhile, inked an agreement with Noon Energy, another California-based maker of long-lasting batteries, to install systems that can store renewable energy for 100 hours by splitting CO2 into carbon compounds and oxygen and then reversing the process to generate power.
“Ultra-long duration energy storage really helps enable clean, reliable power,” said Amanda Yang, head of clean and renewable energy at Meta. “Four hours can only get you that far.”

Historically, facilities have relied on a mix of diesel generators, natural gas turbines and conventional batteries to keep operations running during grid failures or when renewable power lulls. But adding new fossil-fuel capacity threatens tech companies’ pledges to cut carbon emissions at a time when AI’s climate toll is growing. The installation of gas turbines is also bogged down by persistent supply chain bottlenecks, leaving developers with multiyear wait times for new orders.It’s possible to cobble 100 hours’ worth of backup power by stacking banks of lithium-ion batteries, but that can get expensive. While long-duration storage currently costs more, once deployed at scale, it presents a “very strong cost competitive profile,” according to Yang, though she declined to share specific price comparisons.

Emerging long-duration batteries have other advantages. For example, unlike conventional batteries, many of them don’t use critical minerals such as graphite, which have been caught up in the geopolitical crossfire, according to Lucia Tian, director of advanced energy technologies at Google. And as long-duration storage startups build factories on US soil, domestic production not only helps tech giants strengthen their supply chains but also earns them political goodwill with an administration trying to restore manufacturing jobs.

Aric Saunders, executive vice president of Noon Energy, has experienced the new enthusiasm firsthand. AI data centers now account for roughly half of its planned deployment, up from almost none two years ago, he said.

While other customers such as electric utilities and off-grid communities are also helping drive the adoption of long-duration storage, few possess the speed and financial firepower of AI data centers, Saunders said. “They are the accelerant for the industry.”

Indeed, one such startup, Massachusetts-based XL Batteries, credits its sales to Prometheus Hyperscale, a data center developer, for acting as a stamp of validation. Startups making innovative hardware often require significant working capital to scale capacity, but lenders can be cautious about financing products that have yet to demonstrate strong market demand, said Tom Sisto, the company’s cofounder and chief executive officer.
“The path to bankability is the challenge all emerging technology providers are going to face,” he said. “That’s where some of the AI data centers can help.”
As AI data centers step in as early adopters, the technologies will get tested and costs will fall, benefiting other industries, said Yiyi Zhou, an energy storage analyst at BNEF.

Long-duration batteries could also provide a rare opportunity for Western companies to play catch-up with China in the clean tech arena. While Chinese suppliers dominate lithium-ion batteries, industry watchers say that global leadership for longer-lasting energy storage is up for grabs.
Still, it’s early days and it remains to be seen whether long-duration storage startups can deliver on their promised performance and cost savings as commercial deployment rolls out.
For now, the urgency of finding new energy storage solutions appears to be outweighing that uncertainty.
“To scale new technologies, you need to be able to take some of that risk,” said Tian of Google. “We will never get there if we don’t start.”

items.title: Interest Rate Hike: Warsh Did Well. Where Does the Fed Go Now?
body: Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh had ground to make up on Wednesday — and, for the most part, did what was necessary.

The Fed’s policymakers voted unanimously to raise the federal funds rate by a quarter point, to a range of 3.75% to 4%, and, more important, Warsh gave an intelligible explanation. The confusion caused by the new chairman’s previous statements receded. That’s progress.
Yet to say that challenges remain would be putting it mildly. The economic outlook is extremely uncertain, and monetary policy is still in flux.

Warsh had puzzled investors by talking like an inflation hawk after his appointment in May, then voting against a higher policy rate in July. Worse, his stated reasoning was opaque. The following month, he offered a straightforwardly hawkish assessment at the Jackson Hole central bankers’ conference, which was followed in short order by an elevated inflation reading. With high confidence, investors promptly priced in a rate increase. The Fed was right not to confuse them any further with another hold.

Market expectations aside, the decision was a closer call than the committee’s unanimous vote suggests. Supply shocks continue to keep inflation high, and monetary policy is a questionable way to respond. Amid this volatility, it’s odd that August’s single month of noisy data seemed to carry such weight with the Fed’s officials, most of whom had voted to hold in July.

Warsh, at least, now stands on firmer ground. He emphasized that he isn’t swayed by single data points and is focused instead on the longer-term trend in prices, which he thinks (supply shocks notwithstanding) have been too high for too long. Moreover, he said the economy is strong, at full employment and growing satisfactorily, allowing the Fed to safely prioritize price stability. Unlike in July, his analysis and his policy choices have come into alignment. And, for the moment, the Fed’s policy committee is backing him up.

Investors now want to know what happens next. Attention has shifted to the Fed’s new summary of economic projections, or dot plot — in which, as many analysts put it, policymakers have “penciled in” at least one more rate increase in the coming months. Evidently, Warsh has more work to do in this regard, since he declines to take part in the dot-plot exercise and strongly objects to “forward guidance.” In his view, presumably, nothing is penciled in.

Partly as a result, the connections between incoming data and policy choices (the Fed’s so-called reaction function) are far from resolved. If inflation is trending too high, a quarter-point hike — removing, as Warsh put it, a “dose of accommodation” — is unlikely to suffice. But how much higher, as things stand, would the rate need to be? It would help to know how Warsh and his colleagues assess the neutral rate (which neither adds to nor subtracts from aggregate demand). But Warsh puts this question in the same category as forward guidance: He thinks it’s misguided and not worth addressing.

In short, the clarity that would best serve the economy remains elusive. But let’s not be churlish. The decision to raise the policy rate, despite opposition from the White House, strengthens the Fed’s credibility when it otherwise might’ve been severely strained. And for now, Warsh is making sense.

items.title: To Quit Vaping, Some are Starting to Smoke
body: It’s easy to find angst over vaping online. From TikTok and Instagram to Reddit and Facebook, e-cigarette users trade tips on how to quit, share stories about how they got hooked and count the days since they last hit a vape. And then there’s this idea that’s picking up steam: Start smoking. “All of the reasons that make you want to quit smoking” — on a cold morning, for instance, having to put on shoes and a heavy coat to venture outside — “none of them were there for the vape,” says Shaun Moore, a road-paving superintendent in Utah who turned to smoking last year to quit vaping.

Smoking, these people say, is even more disgusting than vaping, making them less likely to light up. Some roll their own to add another hurdle: “I hate the smell and got some gnarly cigs,” a poster says on Reddit. “It worked!”

E-cigarettes were once hailed as a tool that could end smoking. But as the popularity of vaping has risen, so too has the desire to stop. As early as 2019, a US survey of e-cigarette users found that nearly 70% planned to quit.

Elias Klemperer, a professor at the University of Vermont who studies addiction, has one word of advice for people tempted to drop vapes in favor of cigarettes: Don’t. “Anyone who tries to quit e-cigarettes by switching to cigarettes is doing themselves a tremendous amount of harm by going from a less harmful product to a more harmful product,” Klemperer says.

While it’s hard to gauge how widespread this approach is, new data suggests it’s growing globally. A survey of more than 13,000 UK adults by the British public health charity Action on Smoking and Health found cigarettes were the second-most popular method of quitting vapes, right after nicotine replacement therapies like patches and gum. Almost a fifth of vapers attempting to wean themselves off the habit have tried the method. A survey this year by the New Zealand advocacy group ​​Action for Smokefree 2025 found that 14% of people who started vaping to stop smoking  returned to cigarettes when they wanted to quit vaping.

Researchers blame the problem on a fundamental misperception of the relative risks of the two habits. While nicotine, which causes the addiction and can affect cardiovascular health, is present in both, the physical damage from cigarettes comes primarily from inhaling the smoke of burning tobacco, laden with tar, arsenic and other chemicals. E-cigarettes don’t combust anything, so while studies have found traces of toxic metals and other carcinogens in e-cigarette vapor, they’re generally considered the less harmful option. (Michael R. Bloomberg, founder and majority owner of Bloomberg Businessweek parent Bloomberg LP, has been a longtime champion of curbing tobacco use and has campaigned against flavored e-cigarettes.)

Nonetheless, misconceptions abound. On various internet forums, disaffected vapers tout cigarettes as a form of harm reduction. “Multiple people were like, ‘Cigs are so much worse for you.’ We have literally no idea,” one person wrote on Reddit. And a 2025 survey found that three-quarters of English smokers believed vapes are as harmful as or more harmful than cigarettes, up from just under half in 2015. “I do think we’ll find that vaping is a lot worse than we think it is now,” says Chicago bartender Elizabeth Sierminski, who switched to smoking to quit vaping — a habit she calls “definitely the most addicting thing I ever experienced.”

Part of the problem may be the increasing social acceptability of tobacco. Celebrities such as Charli xcx,  Dua Lipa and Jeremy Allen White can be seen with a cigarette casually dangling from two fingers or tucked between their lips. The October cover of Elle magazine features actress Julia Garner holding a smoke. “Cigfluencers” post about the “cigs that don’t count” — drunk cigs, vacation cigs, prison cigs, casino cigs, hospital cigs — racking up hundreds of thousands of likes online. “The scary thing with social media is that trends within youth culture spread like wildfire,” says  Laura Struik, a professor at the University of British Columbia who researches nicotine dependence.

Vapers tend to be from a generation that didn’t grow up seeing the most dramatic anti-smoking campaigns or watching their elders die of lung cancer. As the visibility of consequences declines and negative messaging recedes, these people may be more likely to light up. “It’s a reasonable hypothesis that when a younger generation coming up is just not encountering all of the harms of smoking firsthand that they would be less aware and attuned to the risks,” says Suzanne Colby, a professor of behavioral sciences at Brown University.

The vaping-to-cigarettes approach also carries less obvious risks: Instead of kicking e-cigs, those who want to quit could ultimately end up addicted to both — compounding the possibility of disease. That’s what happened to Syed, a sales professional in Bengaluru who asked to go by his last name because vaping is illegal, though widely practiced, in India. He picked up bootleg e-cigarettes to replace a pack-a-day smoking habit but relapsed after six months. Today he smokes roughly eight cigarettes a day and vapes in between. “I see other people who do really well in life, and they don’t have an addiction to nicotine,” Syed says. “I do wish sometimes that I never picked up a cigarette.”

items.title: Noncitizens Don't Sway Elections, Even in a Pro-Trump Tally
body: Last month, the Census Bureau published a strange little document claiming that “over 24,000” votes were cast by noncitizens in the 2020 US general election. The anonymous report has come under fire for its provenance and methods: It was reportedly produced outside of regular Census Bureau channels by political appointees and staffers at a think tank with close ties to President Donald Trump, using an approach that, according to one former high-level bureau official, was likely to turn up far more false positives than actual noncitizen voters.

The fact that partisan researchers using methods that probably overstate the problem found evidence of only 24,000 noncitizen voters in 2020 is worth dwelling on, though. Coupled with the report’s estimates of how noncitizen voters were distributed among the states, it amounts to a clear admission by the administration that noncitizen voters did not affect the outcome of the 2020 presidential election.

That’s not how Trump portrayed it, of course. “I WON THE ELECTION!” he wrote in a Truth Social post about the report. But for those more numerate and less delusional who are nonetheless concerned about noncitizen voting, the report offers reassurance. The president’s fevered efforts to prevent voting by noncitizens are aimed at behavior that even Trump-friendly researchers conclude isn’t widespread.

That still leaves a channel through which noncitizens truly do affect elections — by being counted in the US census for purposes of apportioning representatives — and the Trump administration has taken aim at that, too. Its recently announced plan to count only noncitizens with permanent residency status (aka green cards) in the 2030 census appears to be both unconstitutional and a recipe for less accurate population statistics, but at least it’s not based on a delusion.

The Census Bureau study on noncitizen voters involved checking 128 million voter records in a commercial database against administrative records containing information on citizenship status, with the researchers concluding that 0.019% of the voter records “represented noncitizens” at the time of the 2020 election. To protect personal information, the comparison was done using anonymized census personal identification keys that, according to a 2014 Census Bureau paper, have an overall false match rate of 0.185%, or nearly 10 times the supposed noncitizen voting rate. This is what prompted John Abowd, an emeritus professor of economics at Cornell University, who was the Census Bureau’s associate director for research and methodology and chief scientist from 2016 to 2022, to write on LinkedIn that “the alleged ‘noncitizen voters’ are therefore much more likely to be data errors than noncitizen voters.”

But let’s just say all 0.019% truly were noncitizen voters and that the rate was the same for the 32 million 2020 votes not yet examined by the researchers. This would add up to 30,000 noncitizen voters, which if concentrated in a few swing states might have been just enough to have some impact on the presidential race. But according to the report, these noncitizen votes were mostly elsewhere, with 10,300 of the 24,000 in the four most populous states — California, Texas, Florida and New York — where victory margins ranged from 371,686 (Trump’s edge in Florida) to 5.1 million (Joe Biden’s in California). Among states with close results, only in Arizona did the estimated number of noncitizen voters top 1,000 — and at 1,100 it was still far short of Biden’s victory margin of 10,457. There’s also no reason to think all of those supposed noncitizen votes would have gone to Biden. Lots of immigrants vote Republican.

You may feel that the appropriate number of noncitizen voters is zero. On the strength of the Census Bureau report alone, it might be, given the false-match problem, but other evidence does point to an amount greater than zero. New Jersey, for example, recently disclosed that it had mistakenly registered 6,600 noncitizens to vote in 2023 and 2024 in the process of granting them driver’s licenses and non-driver identification cards. Of those, the state reported, 340 had actually voted — which indicates both that the number of noncitizen voters isn’t zero and that it is probably minuscule. For the most part, noncitizens living in the US would like to become citizens or, failing that, at least avoid deportation. They are thus wary of doing anything that could get them into trouble, such as voting when it’s not allowed. In New Jersey, the state registered these people to vote and probably sent them multiple mailings urging them to do so, yet only 5% did.

In the 18th and 19th centuries, many US states did allow noncitizens to vote in state and local elections, and some even in federal elections, with the last laws allowing this repealed amid the anti-immigrant fervor of the 1920s. No state has reversed course since, and in 1996 Congress passed a law forbidding noncitizen voting in federal elections, but in recent years a few municipalities have allowed noncitizens to vote in some local elections — in San Francisco, for example, they can vote for the school board. This is arguably in keeping with this country’s founding principle of no taxation without representation, but it adds complexity for election administrators and is certainly confusing for noncitizens.

Any broad crackdown on noncitizen voting, meanwhile, risks preventing far more US citizens from voting than noncitizens. That would almost certainly have been the case with the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act championed by Trump, which passed the House but has not been able to garner a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate. By requiring every voter to provide proof of citizenship, the legislation would likely disenfranchise tens of millions of native-born Americans who don’t have passports or ready access to their birth certificates (and marriage certificates in the case of women who have taken their husbands’ surnames), with Republicans probably hit harder than Democrats. Basing your policy priorities on false beliefs can lead to results like that, and Trump is lucky that a minority of Senate Republicans have refused to go along.

As already mentioned, noncitizens do still play a significant role in national elections in the sense that they’re counted in the US census, which is then used to determine how many House districts and Electoral College votes each state gets. Both the first and second Trump administrations have looked for ways to exclude some noncitizens from these counts, most recently with a regulatory proposal unveiled this month that would leave out all noncitizens other than permanent legal residents from 2030 census totals. The biggest barrier to such a move is the Constitution, which in its original form infamously called for counting enslaved Americans as three-fifths of a person for apportionment purposes, but since the ratification of the 14th Amendment in 1868 has based representation on “the whole number of persons in each State.” Observers also worry that the proposal and other administration actions regarding the census will compromise the quality of the statistics it produces.

Which states benefit electorally from having large numbers of persons who are noncitizens without permanent-resident status? A Pew Research Center estimate based on 2023 census data concluded that the states with the highest percentages of noncitizen residents here either illegally or under some sort of provisional status were Florida (6.9%), Nevada (6.7%), Texas (6.6%) and New Jersey (6.4%).

That’s two red states, one blue state and a swing state. Most of the other states with unauthorized-immigrant population percentages above the 4.1% national rate are reliably Democratic, but overall I wouldn’t be too confident that excluding such people from the census favors one party over the other. Having such large numbers of people living in the US with no prospect of becoming citizens does seem like a problem, though. My favored solution would be to give more of them a path to citizenship; the Trump administration’s is to throw them out of the country. It’s the responsibility of Congress to define some sort of middle ground. Its last significant attempt to do so foundered in the early 2010s, and a new one can’t come soon enough.

items.title: Sports Banker Jeffrey Kaplan Charts Path From Selling Pickles to NFL's Seahawks
body: Jeffrey Kaplan’s first job at his father’s kosher pickle company in New Jersey was learning how to drive a forklift without leaving a mess on the warehouse floor.
Years later, Kaplan advised on the sale of the family business, and it still ranks it among the most meaningful deals of his career.

“Someone says, what are your best M&A deals?” Kaplan said. “Purchase of the Carolina Panthers, purchase of Marvel by Disney, and the last one was selling my dad’s pickle business to the North Jersey competitor. A big pickle merger. I waived my fee on that.”

Since launching Andalusian Sports Advisors in 2020, Kaplan, 65, and his team have advised on 15 sports deals representing approximately $50 billion in value. Projects listed by the firm include work involving MLB’s Tampa Bay Rays, Everton FC of the English Premier League and the NFL’s Panthers and Philadelphia Eagles.

Most recently, Andalusian advised Sun Microsystems co-founder Vinod Khosla on his $9.6 billion deal for the reigning Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks. Khosla is the team’s chair while his wife, Neeru, will serve as the team’s controlling owner. The couple’s son, Neal, will be the franchise’s vice chair.
There were a lot of anxious moments and Kaplan “really helped us day by day to understand what it takes to win a process like this,” Neal Khosla said in an interview.

The Khoslas’ purchase was backed by wealthy individuals and groups from around the world. The team’s second-largest shareholder is Mark Stevens, Sequoia Capital’s former managing partner who’s worth roughly $11.5 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. Other individuals include the Mexico City-based Aramburuzabala family, Gonzalo Hevia Baillères and Penny Pritzker.

Kaplan contends sports advisory requires navigating league bylaws, delicate family dynamics and finding well-capitalized buyers. Unlike big bank M&A groups that focus on market studies and financial projections, sports deals are “fairly bespoke.”

Before Andalusian, Kaplan ran M&A at Merrill Lynch and Bank of America and then joined billionaire hedge fund manager David Tepper’s Appaloosa Management as chief operating officer. Tepper had a small stake in the Pittsburgh Steelers and when the Panthers became available, Kaplan saw a rare chance for him to move beyond being a minority investor.

“If you want to be a control owner, there’s this franchise in North Carolina that’s being sold by an owner under some pressure,” Kaplan recalls telling his old boss. “My real depth in sports started with Tepper.”
In 2018, the Panthers’ $2.2 billion price was seen by some observers as overpriced. The franchise now has an estimated valuation of about $8 billion, according to Sportico.

Sports team values have surged over the past decade, driven by media rights, scarcity and the entry of institutional investors. NFL franchises that once traded for a few billion dollars are now discussed in the range of $8 billion to $10 billion. Minority stakes in teams, once mostly sold to wealthy local investors, are increasingly marketed to private equity firms, family offices and sovereign wealth funds.

The growth has triggered a rush among advisers trying to establish themselves as indispensable intermediaries. Boutique firms such as the Raine Group, BDT & MSD Partners, Inner Circle Sports, Allen & Co. and PJT Partners have long been active in sports deals. Rival advisers including Moelis, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan have expanded their sports efforts as transaction sizes have grown.
“Everyone is trying to build sports teams,” Kaplan said. “Guess what? There’s no one to hire.”

Over the past six years, Kaplan has built a front line of senior sports executives with connections to leagues and owners. The firm’s roster includes former league and venue specialists, including Jonathan Mariner, a former chief financial officer and chief investment officer of MLB, and Joel Litvin, a former president of league operations at the NBA.
The logic is that teams are scarce, emotionally charged assets with unusually durable revenues. “There’s a Sotheby’s component to owning these things,” Kaplan says.

The biggest future test may be finding enough people willing to sign a check. Even for premium NFL assets like the Seahawks, a valuation of over $9 billion limits potential buyers who can meet league liquidity and personal equity requirements. Earlier this year, ESPN reported that interest in the Seahawks was soft. NFL commissioner Roger Goodell later disputed that.

That dynamic has created new opportunities for advisers capable of assembling investor groups and navigating league approvals. Andalusian increasingly acts not just as a sell-side adviser but also as a capital syndicator, helping connect buyers with institutional investors.
“It’s getting harder to sell teams at higher and higher valuations,” Kaplan said. “Valuations are fine. I can defend them. Capital scarcity is the issue.”

items.title: Merz Makes His Last Stand in Twin German Votes
body: Welcome to Balance of Power, bringing you the latest in global politics. If you haven’t yet, sign up here.
It’s always tempting, but usually wrong, to draw national lessons from regional elections in any of Germany’s 16 federal states.
This Sunday is different.
The outcome of voting in the city-state of Berlin and in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania in the northeast will go a long way toward determining Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s fate.
His future as the head of Europe’s heavyweight nation is on the line, with all the political and economic ramifications that implies.
Merz is a deeply unloved leader, by some measures the least popular chancellor on record.
His dilemma isn’t helped by a set of challenges that would make any politician wilt.
Intense economic competition with China. The collapse of the US-led world order and Donald Trump’s scorn for allies. Russia’s war in Ukraine, and surging energy prices due to hostilities in the Gulf.

All are particularly acute for Germany — still the world’s No. 3 economy — with the scars seen in its beleaguered auto industry, humbled industrial sector and an export engine buffeted by rising protectionism.
Politically, Merz’s misfortune was to ascend to the chancellery last year just as the far-right AfD party capitalized on evaporating support for center forces like his.
But Merz also lacks the common touch of predecessors like Angela Merkel, a fellow Christian Democrat, or Gerhard Schroeder, a Social Democrat.
His hectoring approach to politics, like a supermarket manager attempting to bully voters into purchases they don’t want, unsurprisingly fails to resonate.
His CDU party is polling at record lows nationally, well behind the AfD.
Two weeks back, the CDU suffered a calamitous defeat to an aggressively anti—migrant, nationalist AfD in Saxony-Anhalt.
Polls suggest further humiliations on Sunday.
Merz wants to hold on, yet party officials staring at political oblivion may see it as the tipping point for the chancellor.
Just 16 months in office, Merz already looks out of time.

The US is expected to hold off announcing new tariffs on China and other trading partners until after next week’s summit between Presidents Xi Jinping and Trump, sources say, a delay that could preserve such a threat as leverage in the negotiations. While the reason for the postponement is unclear, Trump has repeatedly used tariff warnings to press trading partners for concessions.

Marco Rubio is the first person to act as both the US’s top diplomat and the president’s national security adviser  since Henry Kissinger a half-century ago — something that comes with a coveted perk: a corner desk in the West Wing and easy access to the Oval Office. Few in Washington expected Rubio to last a year as a Trump subordinate, but as our profile suggests, that loyalty has required him to set aside some of his longest-held political convictions.

Russians are growing fearful that President Vladimir Putin may soon order a massive new mobilization for the war in Ukraine after this weekend’s parliamentary elections. Russia took control of the local businesses of Swiss food giant Nestle and French supermarket chain Auchan under a late-night decree issued by Putin, the Kremlin’s largest takeover of foreign corporate assets since at least 2024 amid rising tensions with Europe.

Trump told Axios he was approaching a “big decision” on whether to re-escalate attacks on Iran, with a meeting with Persian Gulf nations planned for next week in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. A group of UN-backed experts meanwhile found “reasonable grounds” to believe that US forces committed war crimes during the conflict, pointing to two airstrikes including one that hit a primary school in Minab, killing around 150 civilians.

At nearly 12,000 feet above sea level in Tibet, grapes grow against the odds. Pazhu Winery is producing thousands of bottles of chardonnay, ice wine and an indigenous red called Yajiang No. 1. Read about the high-altitude winery here.

Lee Jae Myung ruled out sending troops to the Strait of Hormuz despite pressure from Trump as the South Korean president fights to reverse hemorrhaging public support and get his policy agenda back on track.

Former Malaysian prime minister Najib Razak, a central figure in the country’s biggest corruption scandal, has been allowed to serve the remainder of his jail term under house arrest after spending the last four years in prison following an intervention by the king today.

Brazil’s government announced an increase to social-welfare payments just weeks before a tense election, with polls showing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva tied with his right-wing challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro.

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu will propose a vast effort to control spending and narrow the budget deficit after failing to do so in 2026, setting the stage for a parliamentary battle that risks toppling the government just ahead of presidential elections. France is struggling to get a grip on runaway public finances as economic growth slows sharply and a fragmented legislature pushes back against austerity measures.

Power grids serving more than 100 million North Americans are bracing for a demand surge as unseasonable heat strains electrical equipment scheduled for repairs. Temperatures are running more than 20F above normal in some areas served by the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, with triple-digit heat forecast around the South through at least Sunday, according to the US National Weather Service. The searing weather arrived just as power-plant operators were due to take key systems offline for maintenance.

items.title: Swedish Left, Center Parties Scramble to Form Government
body: Hi, this is Charles in Stockholm. Welcome to our weekly newsletter on what’s shaping economies and investments from the Arctic to the Baltic Sea. You can subscribe here.

Spare a thought for Magdalena Andersson. The past week was an emotional rollercoaster for Sweden’s politicians following a national election that was initially too close to call, and the leader of the center-left Social Democrats must now try to form a government by uniting four very different parties.
Four years ago, this process took 37 days. In 2018, it dragged on for a record 134.

The final count from last weekend’s election put Andersson’s opposition bloc at 176 seats, ahead of the incumbent center-right government’s 173, prompting Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson to resign on Thursday. The result also saw the far-right Sweden Democrats suffer their first-ever electoral reversal since they first ran for parliament in 1998. Down but not out, the anti-immigrant party is still Sweden’s third biggest.

Looking ahead, Andersson’s main sticking point is getting two of her alliance partners — the pro-business Center Party and the former communist Left Party — to reach an agreement on how the country should be governed. The Left, with 8.4% of the vote, insists on a formal cabinet role, while the Center has repeatedly ruled out sitting in government with them.
If those talks ultimately break down we could slide back to a 2018 situation, with Ulf Kristersson and the Sweden Democrats back in play.

A breakdown in talks is what far-right leader Jimmie Åkesson is banking on. Having led the populists for the past two decades, the 47-year-old hasn’t given up on a government seat. Earlier Friday, Åkesson visited parliamentary Speaker Andreas Norlén for some fika — coffee and bundt cake baked with apples, blueberries and rhubarb, the colors of the main parties — to discuss next steps in forming a government. Norlén, who personally made the cake, will meet with all party leaders on Friday before deciding on next steps.

As the race to dominate the obesity drug market shows no signs of relenting, Novo Nordisk CEO Mike Doustdar is making moves he hopes will ensure that the Danish pharmaceutical company stays competitive.

Doustdar has dropped the “Nordisk” from the drugmaker’s name, and flipped the orientation of its logo — a century-old bull — from left to right. More importantly, the CEO has announced that the company will broaden its strategic reach.

Speaking to employees this week, Doustdar said Novo needs to expand its services while keeping patients at the center of its strategy. The ambition is to think beyond individual medicines toward the broader goal of helping people live healthier lives, though what that means commercially remains unclear.

Investors are hoping for more clarity on Monday, when Novo holds its capital markets day in London. As well as strategy, Doustdar is expected to discuss the company’s strategy, drug pipeline and business performance after a series of job cuts and abandoned projects.

The backdrop to the gathering is Eli Lilly’s lead in an obesity market that Novo helped create. To change this, as BMO analyst Evan David Seigerman noted, a new name, logo and slogan will need “true strategic change” behind them. That raises the stakes for Monday, when investors will gauge whether Novo really is entering a new chapter.

As the volatility in the Middle East continues to throw sand in the gears of the world’s supply lines, one Nordic company is reaping the benefits: shipping giant Maersk. Its shares are up around 55% this year and trading at near-all-time-highs as shipping rates remain stubbornly elevated. This flies in the face of  analysts’ projections, as most expected rates to normalize — only one out of 26 analysts tracked by Bloomberg recommended that its clients buy Maersk shares. With Houthi rebels staging attacks around the Red Sea this week, the question is whether Maersk can climb even higher.

While outsiders might associate Norway’s culinary culture with seafood or game, locals would also mention a more modest indulgence: Kvikk Lunsj, which translates to quick lunch, is the country’s “hiking” chocolate, a little biscuit to be eaten on the go or during a pause in outdoor activity. Norway’s six million inhabitants each eat about 12 of these every year, with four consumed just over Easter, when Norwegians typically head to the mountains rather than church.

The wrappers traditionally feature national folklore or the 10 rules for hiking in the mountains. Those include: always tell someone where you’re going, check the weather forecasts beforehand, bring adequate equipment and get back in time. While some say the Kvikk Lunsj resembles a Kit Kat, our correspondents in Oslo say that is completely false. The Kvikk Lunsj is just so much better.

items.title: Bessent Got Ahead of Himself on Japan
body: It was always going to be a stretch for Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda to sound very hawkish. Given that officials have tightened cautiously the past two years, something major would have to change to hike interest rates at a faster pace.

There's little to suggest he’s eager to ditch the incremental approach. One of the most eagerly anticipated BOJ decisions in recent years risks satisfying nobody. Friday’s rate increase, by a quarter point to 1.25%, had looked like a slam-dunk. But even that relatively modest step ran into resistance from a couple of policymakers.

Traders wanting a more forthright signal that additional moves are in the works will be disappointed; the yen sold off as soon as the decision was announced. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who joined Tokyo in intervening to support the Japanese currency, had piled pressure on the BOJ to stem the yen’s steep decline. The sharp rally after the joint US-Japan effort in July needed an added extra to retain momentum. Bessent implied something special was in the works, asserting that he had information that the market didn't. If so, it didn’t come this week. He was bullish to a fault.

Chances that Ueda would disappoint were considerable; he has a history of being vague and rambling in his press conferences. Friday was no exception. The statement that preceded his briefing repeated a prior assessment that rates will need to keep climbing to ensure inflation doesn’t accelerate far beyond the 2% target. It was absent of any firm indication that multiple hikes will occur before year’s end. Short of drafting the communique himself, there’s not much Bessent can do to move an entire board. Still, it’s unlikely his scrutiny will come to an end any time soon.

Inflation isn’t about to run away in Japan and, while growth is decent, it’s not booming. While he declined to rule out future steps like a 50 basis point move or tightening at successive meetings, Ueda wasn’t going to be pushed further — or beyond what the board could support. Two officials, both appointed by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, dissented in favor of no change. That might signal that the premier’s team are ambivalent about higher borrowing costs, however much they appreciate Washington’s support.

Japan certainly has company when it comes to raising rates. Peers have either hiked or are likely to in the near future. The European Central Bank moved last week, and traders are counting on another step before year-end. The Federal Reserve nudged rates up on Wednesday and signaled the prospect of at least one further move. Higher energy prices may push the Bank of England to tighten.

The BOJ is now part of a Group of Seven cycle. That's an important shift and one that has eluded Japan for a long time. The mere suggestion that the nation might have something approaching normal policy settings is a victory for Ueda, who came to office three years ago with a distaste for the negative rates that his predecessor imposed in 2016. Consider this: When was the last time Japan didn’t have the lowest rate in Asia, a crown that now belongs to Thailand? Even in the unlikely event that Ueda makes no further moves during the remaining two years of his term, he can say that he's leaving the economy on firmer footing than he found it.

Ueda himself, in his most hawkish comments, signaled that the BOJ was now in a new “phase” of policy conduct, more focused on the need to prevent prices from rising too far above its 2% goal than seeking to boost prices toward it. That’s a big claim for a country that has still not officially declared itself out of deflation.

Bessent called for an end to the easy-money policy of Abenomics and Ueda’s predecessor, Haruhiko Kuroda, calling on Japan to “stop the reflation.” But browbeating the BOJ might miss the point of the nation’s current trajectory. “Reflationary policies that simply boost aggregate demand — like Abenomics — are already a thing of the past,” Takuji Aida, chief economist at Credit Agricole and a member of a panel advising the prime minister, said in a note.

BOJ chiefs frequently attend the Fed’s summer retreat in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, each August. Ueda wasn't able to make it last month, but had he been there, he would have heard Fed Chair Kevin Warsh joke about the natural beauty outside the venue. Some attendees prefer gentle strolls along a trail. Others are up for more vigorous hikes. Choose your path carefully, Warsh advised.
Ueda may yet pick up the pace, but a gravity-defying series of increases is out of character. There’s an argument for just being in the game.

items.title: Turkey Investment Funds: How Pusula, Tera Crisis Sparked Market Panic
body: Turkish citizens piled into some high-profile investment funds in recent years, lured by extraordinary gains that would make many finance professionals pause.

Some of these funds offered triple-digit percentage returns or more, fueling suspicion that they were being artificially inflated. In late 2025, regulators began to take a closer look. By mid-September, the concerns had morphed into a full-blown panic as investors rushed to withdraw their money.

Share prices plunged, forcing the firms to sell more assets to raise cash, threatening a cycle of further losses and withdrawals. More than 350,000 people’s savings were exposed to the liquidated funds, and regulators were trying to convince investors that the damage could be contained.

Finance executives in Turkey have long warned about the suspiciously high returns offered by some funds. The flagship fund of Tera Portfoy Yonetimi AS, for example, returned more than 66,000% in the three years to Sept. 16.

In November 2025, Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek acknowledged allegations of manipulation at some funds, without naming them, and pledged to act. The situation also caught the eye of global index providers including MSCI and FTSE, which warned that distorted share price movements were a threat to Turkey’s prized “emerging market” investment status.

In August, national markets regulator SPK moved into action, releasing a new set of guidelines aimed at easing investor concerns over the unusual stock moves. This triggered sharp outflows from some funds. One of these, Pusula Portfoy Yonetimi AS, saw the value of its share holdings crash and it subsequently defaulted, saying it was unable to meet redemption requests.
Read more: Turkey’s Markets Regulator Tightens Rules for Hedge Funds

Tera swiftly announced it would buy the investment firm, but questions continued to swirl over how it would honor redemption demands. Investors in Tera’s funds panicked, and on Sept. 16 the firm said it, too, would be unable to make payments to clients seeking an exit.

Investors pulled about 213 billion liras ($4.7 billion) from the nation’s investment funds between Aug. 31 and Sept. 16, according to fund tracker Fintables. Turkish stocks suffered their biggest slump in more than a year on Sept. 15.

Tera Chairman Emre Tezmen said the firm was facing an “extraordinary and unprecedented” speculative attack that risked spreading across the markets, in a post on X. In an effort to restore confidence and demonstrate that the weakness was confined to just a few firms, the SPK ordered the liquidation of 131 funds run by seven asset management firms.

On Sept. 17, government officials pledged to roll out measures to head off a liquidity crunch and said there was no risk to Turkey’s wider financial system. The benchmark Borsa Istanbul 100 stock index reversed losses. However, a majority of the stocks in the benchmark index continued to decline, with more than 100 falling by almost the regulatory daily limit of 10%.
Tera said it would cooperate fully with regulators to ensure the interests of its investors are protected. Some other companies issued statements saying they were not facing liquidity problems.

They concentrated their investments in illiquid, low-free-float stocks, where a limited supply of tradable shares made it easy to inflate the price. That meant relatively small purchases could drive the shares sharply higher, making their valuations easier to influence. They then used the inflated stock as collateral to take out short-term loans, which they reinvested in the same stocks, according to finance experts who’ve looked at the trading.
Read more: Behind the 40,000% Stock Surge That’s Mystifying Traders in Turkey

As word spread of the funds’ outlandish returns, more savers piled in, boosting their value further. When the regulator’s new guidelines prompted investors to offload some of the underlying stocks, prices tanked, leading to the wave of fund redemption requests.

More conventional money-market funds were also affected, as some of the firms in question were lending to those funds via so-called reverse repo transactions and taking in wildly inflated stocks as collateral. When the value of those stocks plunged, there was no longer enough money to pay back investors in the money-market funds. Funds also held some blue-chip stocks, and sold them for liquidity, leading to a drop in the wider market.

Istanbul-based OMG Capital Advisors Chief Executive Officer Murat Gulkan said losses were likely to continue in the smaller companies at the center of the crisis. “These assets would fetch pennies on the dollar in the event of an arms-length sale to a third party,” he said.
Top executives at the affected funds have not commented on the allegations since the crisis broke.

The SPK banned some market players from trading while it investigated allegations of share-price manipulation. The market regulator followed up with the order to liquidate funds, including at Pusula and Tera. It filed criminal complaints and issued two-year trading bans on some fund managers at the two firms.
The Financial Stability Committee, chaired by Simsek, said it would focus for now on averting a potential liquidity crunch, and said that the troubles were “temporary and manageable.”

The central bank also stepped in, increasing funding via its weekly repo auctions and raising lenders’ borrowing limits on the interbank money market. It began outright purchases of lira bonds, seeking to prevent a spike in yields amid the market volatility.
The funds due to be liquidated had total assets of more than $18 billion and some 350,000 investors.

On Sept. 18, the SPK said private Is Bankasi AS and state-run Ziraat Bankasi AS would oversee the liquidation, with the process to be completed within three months. The banks will sell assets held by the funds in stages and transfer the cash to investors in proportion to their holdings, according to the regulator.
Analysts said the contagion was largely limited for now to smaller stocks and the seven asset managers that were pumping them. The challenge ahead was to regain the trust of investors.
“Confidence in funds has been seriously damaged,” said Onur Duygu, founder of funds analysis platform Fon Turkey. “Bringing investors back into the fund ecosystem could take a long time.”

items.title: Turkey Fund Rout Erases $4 Billion From a Rapidly-Won Fortune
body: For a long time, it seemed little could stop Altunc Kumova, a discreet businessman who became one of Turkey’s richest people after a meteoric rise in his finance firm’s stock.

That all came to an abrupt end this week after the company Kumova owned was one of the worst hit by the nation’s market gyrations and he, along with other top fund executives, was detained as part of an investigation into mass fund outflows.

Kumova controls 74% of Destek Finans Faktoring AS, a finance company that’s lost almost one-third of its value in three days after defaults in some investment funds triggered a market rout and Turkey’s regulator began a widespread crackdown on the fund-management industry. The decline wiped almost $4 billion off Kumova’s paper fortune, which had stood at about $13.8 billion earlier this week.
Events then took an even more dramatic turn late Thursday when Kumova was detained along with several other figures from fund-management firms.
Read more: Turkey Detains Top Fund Executives, Imposes Travel Bans

Destek is one of multiple companies in the orbit of Tera Yatirim Menkul Degerler AS, an Istanbul-based brokerage and asset-management firm that came under intense scrutiny from regulators in recent months, spilling over this week. The Capital Markets Board moved to liquidate almost $20 billion of funds overseen by Tera and other firms while filing criminal complaints and trading bans against them, alleging price manipulation in shares including Destek.
Kumova didn’t respond to a phone call and WhatsApp message. Bloomberg didn’t receive a response to an email sent to Destek.

Destek shares tumbled 27% in three days, the biggest contributor to a 4% drop for the Borsa Istanbul 100 Index. The stock traded at 1,984 liras as of 10:36 a.m. in Istanbul for a market capitalization of 661 billion liras, valuing Kumova’s stake at about $10 billion.

Kumova wealth drop places him alongside Hamdi Ulukaya, the Turkey-born founder and chief executive officer of Greek yogurt company Chobani who’s worth $10.1 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Destek operates in invoice factoring, a form of finance that involves buying the bills that are owed to companies and then securing payment from the parties they supplied. Founded in 1996, it’s part of a wider group of companies controlled by Kumova including a bank, according to its website.

The company generated net income of 2.6 billion lira for the first half of 2026, filings show. Destek’s price-to-earnings ratio, a metric comparing market value with reported profit, is about 132 times while JPMorgan Chase & Co., the biggest US bank, is at 15 times, Bloomberg data show.
Tera arranged Destek’s initial public offering in 2025. A Tera investment fund also became the company’s biggest shareholder after Kumova, data show.

Led by Chairman Emre Tezmen — who received a travel ban as part of the recent crackdown — Tera has been the talk of Istanbul’s financial circles for minting gains that seemed impossible by normal standards. Its flagship investment fund returned more than 66,000% over a three-year span, fueled by a strategy of pouring billions of lira into a tight circle of related companies and amplifying the bets with borrowed cash.
Read More: Turkey Turns to Two Big Banks to Liquidate Troubled Funds

In August, regulators tightened rules on investment funds holding concentrated bets in illiquid stocks. That forced funds to sell some of their positions and triggered a run to the exits. Funds at Tera Portfoy — Tera’s investment-fund subsidiary — and Pusula Portfoy Yonetimi AS announced in recent days that they’ve been unable to meet client redemptions.

items.title: BOE's Balance Sheet Move Eases Repo Pressure, Barclays Says
body: The Bank of England’s plans to slow the pace of its bond sales will ease pressure on repo operations as well as providing a tailwind for strained long-end gilts, according to a Barclays Plc strategist.

The move has “created a very positive environment for long-dated gilt spreads and the long end of the curve by creating a genuine shortage of paper that is unlikely to be alleviated any time soon,” Barclays’ Moyeen Islam wrote in a note. The BOE is also “implicitly taking some of the operational pressure off its repo operations.”
Read more: Bank of England Eases Bond-Market Pain With Gilt Sales Overhaul

The BOE’s short-term repo facility provides sterling in return for pledging gilts as collateral. Those operations had been expanding faster than reserves were being drained through the BOE’s asset purchase facility, which holds the bonds that were purchased during the BOE’s quantitative easing program.

Slowing the balance sheet runoff should allow both short- and long-term repo operations to grow more gradually, giving the BOE greater control over the banking system’s moves toward its equilibrium level of reserves.

Some gilts could become increasingly scarce. Of the seven bonds maturing between 2029 and 2034 that remain in the BOE’s legacy holdings, six have 30% to 50% of their outstanding stock held in the asset purchase facility, according to Barclays calculations. With little prospect of new supply, fewer may be available to trade or borrow over time, making them relatively more expensive and more sought-after in repo markets.

Some of the longer bond holdings in the asset purchase facilities could become candidates for the UK Debt Management Office’s tender program. This sells non benchmark bonds to ease dislocations and tap lower yields.

Islam said there are still kinks within this new system to be ironed out, including what the DMO will do with the gilts it receives. He said the September minutes “obliquely allude to the MPC discussing the DMO’s ‘ability to retire bonds,’ but this is something that would have to be done in consultation with the market.”
Read more: ‘Hurried’ QT Decision Suggests BOE Is Concerned About Gilts: BMO

items.title: FX Market Is Reliably Calm Even as the World Gets More Volatile
body: Currency volatility has been so low for so long that traders are starting to treat it as the new normal rather than a passing phase.

That subdued backdrop was among the major themes at an annual industry gathering in Amsterdam this week for a second year running, with investors describing a market where sharp changes in bonds, oil and geopolitics still struggle to generate lasting currency swings.

“What we are lamenting is a secular downtrend in currency volatility,” said Harish Neelakandan, co-chief investment officer at AlphaEngine Global Investment Solutions, a systematic trend-following fund. “That’s the hand we’ve been dealt. We have to learn to live with this.”

This lack of volatility in the $9.6 trillion-a-day foreign-exchange market is becoming a perennial problem for traders aiming to thrive on big swings. Yet the calmer environment is likely to be beneficial for asset managers and companies looking to hedge their exposure.

Neelakandan said greater coordination between central banks has helped contain currency moves, leaving geopolitical shocks to produce only brief bursts of volatility. Unless that backdrop changes fundamentally, traders are likely to keep treating such spikes as opportunities to short volatility once again.

“What we’re seeing is the ‘nothing ever happens’ trade, where people just keep selling volatility,” said Thomas Carreau, a currency portfolio manager at CN Investment Division, which manages Canadian National Railway’s pension fund.
Read more: Traders Blame ‘Insane’ Tech Advancements for Quiet FX Markets

Even recent yen moves have remained relatively contained, Carreau said. The currency has been in the spotlight in recent months after sliding to the weakest in four decades before joint US-Japanese intervention to support it caused a series of sharp rallies.

He added that carry trades, where investors borrow in low-yielding currencies to buy higher-yield assets, continue to perform well. He prefers to structure them to be dollar neutral because US President’s Donald Trump’s social media posts can still cause small day-to-day swings in the US currency. It’s a strategy that performs well when volatility is low.
“Carry is king,” he said.
Read more: Carry Traders Eye Franc, Krona as Yen’s Funding Appeal Ebbs

The prolonged calm does pose some risk. Harel Jacobson, associate portfolio manager at hedge fund Capstone Investment Advisors, said lower volatility forces traders to put on larger positions to generate the same returns, leaving portfolios more exposed when a rare big move hits.

“What you end up with is a ticking time bomb sitting on your portfolio,” said Jacobson. His fund routinely buys cheap hedges designed to protect against unusually large market moves, pointing to last year’s surge in the Taiwan dollar as the kind of event they are looking to cover.
Low volatility isn’t necessarily bad news for everyone. It can also reflect a liquid and efficient market that continues to absorb shocks in a volatile world.
“The world might not be reliable, but the FX market is,” said the conference chair Allan Guild, director of Hilltop Walk Consulting.

Companies are adapting their strategies. Georgios Velissariou, head of financial risk management at Hitachi Energy’s group treasury, said lower volatility had made options a more attractive way to hedge certain currency exposures.

Meanwhile for some banks, the environment is prompting a rethink of parts of their operations. Karel Sanders, head of FX product management at Rand Merchant Bank, said dollar-rand volatility at a two-decade low was forcing the South African lender to reconsider how it runs its options business.
“Do we stay principal market makers in FX volatility, or do we become an agency business? We’re leaning more towards an agency business,” he said.

There were also signs on the conference floor that traders were looking beyond traditional FX for action. At one stand, attendees were tempted by sweet Dutch waffles to vote on which currency pair would move the most over the main day. The winner was silver against the dollar.
A market increasingly built around low volatility may be poorly protected on the rare occasions when that calm breaks. Some see little incentive to prepare.
“The market finds itself in a situation where we don’t know what the catalyst will be for the next blow up and no one is positioned for it, because if you’re early you’re wrong,” said Carreau.

items.title: NSE's $2.4 Billion India IPO Fully Subscribed on Second Day
body: The $2.4 billion initial public offering of National Stock Exchange of India Ltd. was fully subscribed on the second day of bidding, bringing the world’s busiest derivatives exchange by volume closer to completing one of the biggest listings in the country’s history.

Bids exceeded the 88.6 million shares on offer, with the portions reserved for institutional and wealthy investors each covered 1.3 times, according to data on the BSE Ltd.’s website as of 2:45 p.m. local time. Retail investors bid for nearly 65% of the shares set aside for them.

Full subscription brings NSE to the brink of completing a long path to the IPO dating back to 2016, when the exchange first filed. The plan was delayed for years amid regulatory and governance issues.
Read More: NSE Slashes IPO Ambitions as World’s Biggest Options Boom Fades
NSE is offering shares at 1,700 rupees to 1,785 rupees apiece, with bidding scheduled to close on Sept. 21. The offering consists entirely of stock sold by existing shareholders.

At the top end of the range, the offering would raise about 226 billion rupees ($2.4 billion), making it India’s largest IPO after Hyundai Motor India Ltd.’s 279 billion-rupee share sale in 2024. The price would value NSE at about 42.9 times its earnings for the year ended March. While that’s a discount to domestic rival BSE Ltd., it’s well above the roughly 24 to 25 times earnings multiple for some of the world’s largest listed exchanges.

The exchange has the potential to emerge as a company that shows steady growth over the long term and could become a meaningful holding in investors’ portfolios, according to Thomas J. Priju, a portfolio manager at Karma Capital. In the near term, a resolution of the issues around the new closing auction mechanism could provide an additional catalyst, he said.

Still, one of the biggest risks is tighter regulatory scrutiny of speculative derivatives trading, a business central to NSE’s profitability. Options trading accounted for about 60% of operating revenue in the year ended March, leaving the exchange exposed to measures aimed at curbing activity in the segment.

Before opening its order book, NSE received the buy-in of anchor investors who committed 67.46 billion rupees. They included global funds like Goldman Sachs, HSBC, Fidelity, Eastspring, as well as sovereign wealth funds GIC Singapore and Abu Dhabi Investment Authority. Among local firms, Life Insurance Corp., SBI Funds Management Ltd and ICICI Prudential Asset Management Co. were some of the largest anchor investors in the offering.

items.title: The US Wants China to Know It Has Weapons in Space
body: In a surprising statement this week, Secretary of the Air Force Troy E. Meink revealed that the US has weapons in space. He said, “We are increasing readiness against existing threats, and the United States has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action.”

The surprise was less the substance than the decision to say it publicly. Military analysts have long assumed that the US possessed sophisticated counterspace capabilities, but the Pentagon had never acknowledged deploying weapons in orbit.

Meink, an Air Force veteran with a Ph.D. in aeronautical engineering, is an expert on space-based communications and intelligence systems. He did not discuss any details about what kinds of weapons are in orbit. There was no chance his remarks would go unnoticed: They came at the Air, Space & Cyber Conference, a high-profile annual gathering of military leaders and defense contractors in Maryland.
Why did he decide that this was an appropriate time to abandon Washington’s longstanding ambiguity about weapons in orbit?

First, as Meink said, talking about space weapons may serve as a deterrent against China and Russia. Both are likely moving ahead with systems that can put at risk America’s most valuable satellite constellations, which provide precise navigation, clear communications and high-grade intelligence-gathering.

Moscow and Beijing are testing or deploying maneuverable satellites, high-energy lasers and antisatellite missiles. Most alarming, Moscow may be developing a space-based nuclear weapon that could use electromagnetic pulses to disrupt or destroy US satellites across a wide area.
Given this rising threat, publicly signaling that the US can retaliate or protect its satellites will serve as a deterrent.

A second reason for the secretary’s revelation may be to build momentum for “Golden Dome,” President Donald Trump’s signature effort to build a missile shield around the entire US. It is a project of enormous scale and challenge, reminiscent of Ronald Reagan’s Strategic Defense Initiative, the never-realized “Star Wars” project.

Meink also highlighted the military’s progress on space-based interceptors that would be part of a national missile defense. Publicly acknowledging that the US has weapons in orbit may make Golden Dome seem more realistic. That’s important, because it has a whopping price tag: The Congressional Budget Office has estimated that a national missile-defense system like Golden Dome would cost $1.2 trillion over two decades; some think tanks such as the American Enterprise Institute have provided estimates of up to $3.6 trillion for more ambitious systems.

Third, the founding of the US Space Force and reestablishment of US Space Command during Trump’s first term has created momentum for space operations generally. The Space Force, the sixth branch of the US armed forces, organizes, trains and equips personnel for military space operations. But with only 15,000 active-duty members, it isn’t always taken as seriously as it should be.

Space Command was created in 1985 but in 2002 folded into US Strategic Command, which oversees the nuclear arsenal. The Trump administration revived Space Command as one of the 11 unified combatant commands, providing an operational center of gravity for the new Space Force. Counterintuitively and controversially, Space Command is considered a geographic command, with an “astrographic” area of responsibility extending from 62 miles above the earth (the Karman line) to the Moon and beyond.

In the late 1990s, while serving under the Joint Chiefs of Staff, I was present at arguments about whether Space Command should be considered geographic or functional like Strategic Command. Some said, “space is not a place like the surface of the earth, but rather a domain like cyber or the air.” I remember one general countered poetically that its area of responsibility should be “from the skies above the earth to the mind of God.” That’s a big AOR.

In publicly acknowledging the Pentagon’s orbital weaponry while revealing nothing about its scope or capabilities, Meink put America’s adversaries on notice. Ending years of strategic ambiguity about space will only increase deterrence here on Earth.
Stavridis is dean emeritus of the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy at Tufts University. He is on the boards of Aon, Fortinet and Ankura Consulting Group.

items.title: SoftBank Boosts Credit Line to $6.5 Billion as AI Debts Mount
body: SoftBank Group Corp. secured an additional $450 million to increase the size of an existing credit line to $6.5 billion, people familiar with the matter said, giving the Japanese conglomerate more financial flexibility as it expands investments in artificial intelligence.

The previous facility equivalent to $6.05 billion was due to expire this month, and SoftBank will have another year to draw down on the expanded amount, according to the people who asked not to be identified because the information is private. It’s unclear whether SoftBank has tapped the new line or if it plans to do so.

SoftBank is at the epicenter of debates about the future of debt-fueled bets on AI, at a time when market volatility has increased amid safety warnings. One of the world’s biggest investors in the technology, the conglomerate has recently conducted a flurry of deals to finance its push that includes an expanded stake in AI giant OpenAI. In one of the latest examples, SoftBank increased its margin loan backed by shares of its chip unit Arm Holdings Plc by $5 billion to $25 billion.

There are currently more than 20 banks involved for the expanded credit line, the people said. The new deal carries an interest margin of 210 basis points over the benchmark Secured Overnight Financing Rate, they added.
A representative from SoftBank declined to comment.

Commitment or credit lines are revolving loan facilities that lenders make available for a set period. Companies often treat them as liquidity backstops and do not necessarily draw on the funds immediately.

The credit line adds to a wave of debt-raising activities tied to SoftBank’s bet on OpenAI and more broadly, on artificial intelligence. Recent financings include an $11.87 billion term loan and a $10 billion loan backed by its OpenAI stake, despite concerns about growing risks in the sector.
Founded and led by billionaire Masayoshi Son, SoftBank is slated to invest close to $65 billion in OpenAI by October.
SoftBank also signed a $40 billion bridge loan earlier this year to finance its OpenAI investments. The Japanese firm paid the entire outstanding balance of $25.9 billion on that borrowing this week.

The company has drawn down $30 billion from the bridge loan but it hasn’t given any guidance if it will take the remaining $10 billion. The next time it can do so is in early October, the people said.

The company has also been meeting with fixed-income investors in New York this week to test appetite for a possible junk bond offering that could total $10 billion to $20 billion, people familiar with those discussions have said. A deal could come to the market as early as next week, according to other people briefed on the matter.
“We have investor meetings to provide an update in New York on a non-deal basis. Nothing has been determined on bond issuance,” SoftBank said when asked about the meeting.

Separately, Apollo Global Management Inc. is in talks with SoftBank about boosting the size of a loan to $9 billion from $5.4 billion to help the Japanese firm finance its investment in OpenAI, people familiar with the deal said earlier this week.

Debate has been intensifying over the pace of AI development and the risks associated with increasingly powerful systems. Some executives are now voicing the need to slow the pace of development due to escalating risks from the technology. OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman has said that his company wouldn’t proceed with a public offering this year as it addresses safety-related concerns.
The cost of insuring SoftBank’s debt against default has climbed this year, with credit-default swaps marking a three-year high earlier this week.

items.title: Is It Really AI End Times or Just 'Cognitive Surrender'?
body: Listen and subscribe to Everybody’s Business on Apple , Spotify, iHeart and the Bloomberg Terminal.

Senior tech executives spent the past few weeks loudly warning of the risks posed by artificial intelligence. Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei — who has been furiously racing to develop ever-more human-like chatbots ahead of a potential initial public offering — published an essay suggesting instead that the industry needs to slow down or risk eradicating all human beings. (Apparently some Anthropic employees put that possible outcome at around 10%.)

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he also favored a slowdown, and SpaceX’s Elon Musk concurred, sketching out a nightmare scenario. “If it were able to take control of military systems and, say, launch a nuke,” he said of AI, “that would be bad.”

Critics have pointed out there are aspects of these warnings — and previous warnings from the AI giants — that are potentially self-serving. For instance, they draw attention from more immediate risks, such as AI-generated scams, the proliferation of AI “slop” and the fact that college students are relying on chatbots to such an extent that administrators warn of “cognitive offloading” and “cognitive surrender.”

This week on Everybody’s Business, journalist Vauhini Vara joins to discuss a potential solution: software that promises to sort slop from the real thing. In the latest issue of Bloomberg Businessweek, Vara profiled Pangram, a startup whose founders contend we’ll eventually rely on detectors to avoid AI text in the same way we use spam filters to avoid junk email. Pangram is controversial, partly because it essentially offers an AI solution to AI problems, but also because critics have warned of the danger of false positives.

But Vara found that Pangram seems to offer an impressive level of reliability — or at least a low rate of false positives. It’s also, she says, somewhat different from the large language models it attempts to detect, in the sense that its own models are smaller and its founders have licensed the content they’ve scanned (in contrast to the main chatbot operators, which ingested huge quantities of copyright-protected text and video without initially paying licensing fees). Pangram has been popular on social media as a way to shame writers who may have  done a little bit of cognitive offloading, but it’s especially popular among college professors, who use it as a starting point to enforce a no-AI writing policy.

Also this week, we explore a possible fan backlash to the sudden influx of private equity cash into sports with Bloomberg reporter Randall Williams. As long as pro-football and other major sports continue to post huge ratings, and as long as franchise values soar, investors will look for sports investments. But there are hints of fan resistance in the National Basketball Association’s reaction to  alleged salary cap manipulation by the league’s wealthiest owner, and the swift demise of the plan to sell part of the World Cup to a   vehicle connected to the Kushner family.

Finally, we discuss Kevin Warsh’s decision to act like a conventional Federal Reserve chair, bucking pressure from Donald Trump, and Coyote vs. ACME, a David and Goliath story within a David and Goliath story that is also, maybe, the perfect movie for the current political moment.

About the show: every week, hosts Stacey Vanek Smith and Max Chafkin take a look at the week’s business news and break down what you need to know with the help of Bloomberg journalists, experts and the people and businesses trying to navigate the economy every day.
