items.title: Iran War, Tariffs and Trump's Second-Term Quest to Be Consequential
body: Rarely has the post-World War II global order felt so messy. America’s six-month-long war against Iran has entrenched the Islamic regime, closed the Strait of Hormuz and sent oil prices  soaring. Despite Donald Trump’s promise that he’d end the conflict in Ukraine “on Day 1,” it rages unabated. Meanwhile, the president constantly swaps US enemies and allies, wooing North Korea’s Kim Jong Un while weakening ties with South Korea, making fresh threats to wrest control of Greenland from NATO member Denmark, and instigating a trade war and an absurd Great Lakes-naming tussle with America’s erstwhile friend to the north, Canada.

One of Trump’s favorite words these days to describe his own presidency is “consequential.” He wants to be seen as a historic leader who remapped the world and shifted the tectonic plates of history. At home, that’s meant erecting monuments, demolishing a wing of the White House to make way for a ballroom over a chorus of legal and practical objections, and renaming places for both himself and the US at a steady clip. Abroad, trying to preordain his own legacy has required waging economic warfare on an unprecedented scale and, in cases where that hasn’t worked on an acceptable timeline, such as Venezuela and Iran, using military force. But foreign countries and their leaders aren’t as easily coerced as US lawmakers. And Trump’s second-term quest to be consequential looks poorly conceived and, at least for now, nothing short of catastrophic.

The president’s crusade intensified on April 2, 2025, when he signed an executive order announcing sweeping tariffs on imports. China answered these so-called Liberation Day tariffs by rolling out its own levies and restrictions on US goods and withholding access to rare earths that are vital to manufacturing in aerospace, defense and other industries. At the same time, European nations, feeling jilted by a longtime partner, deepened their relationships in South America, Asia and the Middle East. Countries found they didn’t need America to the extent they once thought.

Instead, the primary victim of Trump’s tariffs wound up being America itself. US companies and their customers had to pay the levies, while business leaders were left to survey a more hostile landscape abroad, with long-standing allies searching for backups to America’s artificial intelligence models, cloud computing services and even the dollar. “You basically have the entire world eager now to build workarounds to the US financial system,” says Edward Fishman, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and the author of Chokepoints: American Power in the Age of Economic Warfare. “It’s not just problematic from an American power standpoint, it’s problematic for our businesses and for American economic dynamism.”

When economic pressure was ineffective, Trump’s quest to be consequential required a more forceful approach. That worked in Venezuela in January, when Special Forces neatly extracted President Nicolás Maduro and his wife from Caracas and installed a leader more inclined to give the US access to its prodigious oil reserves. Emboldened by their success, Trump and his advisers then tried to run the same playbook in Iran. Acting in concert with Israel, they killed Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, significantly set back the country’s nuclear program — and prodded Iran to use its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, the conduit for about 20% of the world’s oil shipments.

In trying to leave a lasting mark on the map in his second term, Trump has learned that coercion doesn’t always deliver the desired result. Sovereign countries aren’t easily steamrolled, and exerting pressure can be counterproductive — solidifying support for even unpopular leaders and hardening their resolve. Cuba, another country on Trump’s regime-change wish list, is a 70-year-old object lesson in the high pain tolerance of authoritarian nations bent on challenging American hegemony. Democracies, on the other hand, tend to have a comparatively low pain threshold. They wobble at the first sign of higher fuel prices, a slowing economy and, especially, wartime casualties.

One question the October issue of Bloomberg Businessweek poses is what kind of political price will be paid by Trump’s top foreign affairs advisers, primarily Marco Rubio, the secretary of state. As a senator, Rubio was an internationalist who seemed to have a good handle on the limits of economic statecraft and military intervention. But unlike his predecessors in Trump’s first term, who tried to counterbalance his impetuous whims, Rubio has ubjugated his expertise and sees his job as helping to execute the president’s “America First” vision of the world. If circumstances in the Middle East don’t improve by the US election in 2028, there will almost certainly be a backlash against anyone associated with that approach.

It’s always possible the wind could shift in Trump’s — and Rubio’s — favor. Iran’s economy is in shambles, its new leader hasn’t been seen in months, and its proxies in Gaza and Lebanon have been weakened. “If at the end of this we have a stronger NATO because the Europeans are finally doing their own part for defense, and we’ve got different regimes in Venezuela, Cuba and Iran, that is a different global map than when Trump came in,” says Matthew Kroenig, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Scowcroft Center for Strategy and Security and an adviser to Rubio’s 2016 presidential campaign. “But we’re not there yet. There’s still a lot of stuff that could go wrong.”

For now, Trump’s quixotic crusade to be considered one of history’s “great men” has awakened friends and foes alike to their own leverage over the US. It’s had consequences for sure. They’re just not the ones he imagined.Read next: Marco Rubio Remakes Himself as Trump’s MAGA Warrior

items.title: Diesel Is Coming for Trucking, Your Home - and the Midterms
body: US energy politics usually begin and end with gasoline prices. Those are at a seasonal record, but even $4.44 a gallon pales against diesel, now at an all-time high of $6.40. Most drivers’ eyes skim over that bit of the price sign — it’s called a gas station, after all — but America can’t afford to look away. Diesel isn’t just an immediate price (and politics) problem; it’s building up vulnerabilities for the US on several fronts that will play out through winter and into 2027.

A barrel of crude oil gets refined into different products such as gasoline, naphtha and so forth. One is “distillate fuel oil,” which consists of transportation diesel — about 75% of the total — along with fuel oil to heat homes and run generators and other industrial processes. The US uses about 3.9 million barrels of distillate a day, on average. That is far less than gasoline’s 8.8 million barrels. But diesel is the fuel of commerce, powering trucks, trains, tractors and more besides, meaning its price ripples into everything: logistics, manufacturing, agriculture, construction — even data centers.

This adds another sticky element to already stubborn inflation that, as my Bloomberg Opinion colleague  Jonathan Levin wrote recently, risks unmooring broad price expectations. Brief jumps in diesel can be passed on with temporary surcharges on freight contracts, but a sustained increase will ultimately get embedded in those contracts and hit kitchen tables as it flows down the supply chain.

The current increase has legs. Crude oil at $100-plus due to the Iran war is a big factor. JP Morgan Chase & Co.’s commodities analysts just threw their hands up on predicting where that goes, writing  “we simply don’t know how to model the endgame.”

But this clearly isn’t just about crude oil; it is also about refining, with diesel futures trading around $214 a barrel (retail equates to almost $269). The price difference between diesel and crude oil futures, or the “crack spread,” is now about $112 a barrel, higher than the price of crude itself — which is most unusual.

Alongside crude oil, the Iran war has also disrupted regional refinery production and fuel shipments. Ukraine’s drone attacks on Russian refineries have strengthened at the same time, to the point where President Donald Trump recently tried to shift the blame for expensive diesel to Kyiv (you may recall that Ukraine has reason to target Russia’s refineries). Russian and Middle Eastern diesel exports in August were together down 75%, year on year, the International Energy Agency estimates. Globally, refinery runs were down 4.2 million barrels a day.
When refineries aren’t running, stocks get drawn down. Things have been a little different in the US, though: Refineries are running flat out but stocks have still plunged.

The US had about 104 million barrels of distillate in storage at the end of August — the lowest level for that month since the early 1950s, when demand was a third of today’s level. Distillate demand rises from here to its winter peak, partly because of harvesting and households burning heating oil, primarily in northeastern states. New England, where stocks are around the lowest on record, best hope this winter isn’t like the last one.

Those huge crack spreads, though, mean US refineries are having a golden year; it is the leading S&P 500 sub-sector by far, up 141% to date. They are working harder, and for longer, than usual, with utilization running north of 95% all summer.

Diesel exports have risen, though, as other countries disrupted by geopolitical ructions bid for US barrels. There is a growing risk for oil companies that Trump, ally though he may be, panics about prices ahead of the midterm elections and bans fuel exports (see this). This week’s comment from Senate Majority Leader John Thune that he is “open to exploring” the idea won’t have gone down well in Houston.

The basic problem, however, is that there are only so many US refineries. Energy Secretary Chris Wright has mused about invoking the Defense Production Act to boost capacity. Federal funding conceivably might help reopen a recently closed refinery, such as Valero Corp.’s Benicia plant in California, analysts at ClearView Energy Partners point out, or even the “long-challenged” Limetree Bay facility in the US Virgin Islands. But none of that would be overnight. As for brand new refineries, any developer must weigh a multi-decade investment against flat US oil demand and federal energy policy that has swung from pro-fossil fuels to green energy and back again in the space of one decade.

Running refineries harder for longer, meanwhile, builds up a deficit of deferred maintenance. Utilization has been higher than average all year, and the fall maintenance season may be trumped by those high cracks. That risks teeing up disruptive unplanned outages next year, when the market might hope to rebuild depleted stocks.

By then, of course, the two wars underlying this crisis may be over. At least one of those is nominally under Trump’s control, and he is clearly aware of the political fallout from high energy prices as the midterms loom. Fuel oil may not be a blanket issue like gasoline, but it heats a lot of homes in several Senate battleground states such as Alaska, Maine and New Hampshire, and its use is more prevalent in rural areas that often skew Republican. Once the smoke clears after the Nov. 3 elections, however, America’s diesel problems will still be mounting.

items.title: Hungary Can Quit Russia Gas, Reviews Nuclear Deal, Minister Says
body: Hungary can meet European Union regulation to completely wean the country off Russian gas in a year’s time, the energy minister said, in a significant shift from the policies pursued under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban.

Hungary has enough pipeline connections to source gas from elsewhere at competitive prices, Economy Minister Istvan Kapitany said in a Telex interview published on Friday. The government is also reviewing the Russian-led expansion of its sole nuclear plant and is in talks with suppliers to diversify crude oil supplies away from Russia.

“If the situation develops the way it currently appears, Hungary’s gas supply can and will be secured from other sources” by October 2027, Kapitany said, citing the date when EU member states must stop natural gas imports from Russia.

The comments signal Prime Minister Peter Magyar’s readiness to break with Orban’s approach to Russia. During 16 years of rule that ended in April’s election, Orban had doubled down on Moscow for energy, even as EU peers moved to end their own reliance following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Orban had argued that landlocked Hungary had no other options to ensure its energy security. Critics had said the policy helped convert Budapest into a tool of the Kremlin, isolating Hungary as Orban sought to block sanctions against Moscow and worked to undermine Western aid for Kyiv in order to please Russia.
Read More: Hungary Expels 10 Russian Diplomats in Break from Orban Era

The Orban government’s decision to scrap an international tender for the expansion of the Paks nuclear plant and to hand the contract to Russia’s Rosatom Corp. in 2014 had been widely seen as the centerpiece of the country’s changing and ever closer ties to Russia.

Kapitany said the project, which is running years behind, is now also under review and that a decision would be made by the end of the year on whether the expansion of the 2,000 megawatt plant is needed at all.
He pointed to technological advances that may allow the country to extend the lifetime of the four current nuclear blocks — which would otherwise expire in 2032 — by another 20 years.

“The review is still ongoing, we’ll finish it by the end of the year and that’s when we’ll make a decision on whether Hungary needs the additional nuclear blocks in its energy mix,” Kapitany told Telex. He said the review was being conducted in an “open-minded and totally objective way.”
Read More: EU Court Puts Hungary’s Russia-Led Nuclear Project in Limbo (1)

Besides diversifying energy sources, Hungary is also aiming to reduce imports, particularly in electricity. Plans include to boost energy storage capacity and to open up the country to major wind power investments.

The country’s energy import reliance has for long been a key economic vulnerability, with global oil and gas price shocks having an outsized impact on the local currency. The forint swung this week as investors assessed whether energy supply concerns from the Middle East crisis may ease.

items.title: NYC's Flatiron Building Welcomes Buyers After Office-to-Residential Conversion
body: Bill Sofield refers to himself as an archaeologist. He is by profession, however, an interior designer, known for the stores he’s done for clients such as Tom Ford and Gucci. For the past 3½ years he’s been working inside the Flatiron Building, one of the most photographed structures in the world, turning it into 37 apartments.

When Sofield walked its first two floors, what he found was wreckage: severed cast-iron staircases that led nowhere, the bolted remains of a boiler, air handlers from another century. The building, one of New York City’s oldest surviving skyscrapers, had stood almost empty for years. His job was to turn the ruins into homes.

Designed by Daniel Burnham and built in 1902 as a construction company’s headquarters at the triangle where Fifth Avenue intersects Broadway, the Flatiron captured the popular imagination almost from the start. Alfred Stieglitz photographed the prow in the fog. Childe Hassam painted it in winter. Postcards from the first decades of the 20th century show women’s skirts lifting in the wind tunnel at the building’s base, an accident of air pressure that popularized one of the era’s more durable scraps of slang: “23 skidoo.” (That’s what police told the men loitering at the corner of 23rd Street for the view, or so it goes.) Andrew Dolkart, who teaches historic preservation at Columbia University and once worked at the city’s Landmarks Preservation Commission, calls the steel-framed Beaux Arts tower the first building to become a symbol of New York: “It became famous in both high culture and low.”

For 124 years the Flatiron has been celebrated by New Yorkers. Sometime late this fall, it will become home to a select few of them. Buyers have paid from $11 million to more than $50 million for units in the building, where the least expensive apartments are roughly the size of a suburban house. Sixteen of the 37 residences are under contract, according to Corcoran Sunshine Marketing Group, at an average price of $19 million. Over the years the office tower has housed the pulp magazine pioneer Frank Munsey, the puppeteer Tony Sarg, the Imperial Russian Consulate and, for a half-century, Macmillan Publishers. Never residents.

The Flatiron is now one of the crown jewels of a national office-to-residential movement, alongside the Chrysler Building, another similarly storied New York landmark whose owner has publicly proposed converting it into housing. Since the Covid-19 pandemic, tens of thousands of apartments have been carved out of distressed workspaces in American cities. Most of those buildings were bought for pennies on the dollar. Troubled office towers across the country are trading for fractions of their pre-pandemic value. As the Wall Street Journal reported in April, a 485,000-square-foot building in Chicago sold for $4 million. A complex in Denver that had traded for $176 million in 2013 changed hands recently for more than $5 million. The federal government sold an office building in Washington for $24 million, a sliver of its former worth.

But the Flatiron is something different. After a long and contested auction, it sold in 2023 for a little more than $160 million. The Brodsky Organization, one of New York’s established real estate families, is leading the conversion with the Sorgente Group. Dan Brodsky chaired the board of the Metropolitan Museum of Art for 12 years. “They consider this another way they’re giving back to New York,” says James Lansill, the Corcoran Sunshine Marketing Group executive who’s handling sales.

A permit for the Flatiron conversion listed as many as 100 units at nearly 2,000 square feet in size. To some of the building’s admirers, turning a publicly cherished landmark into just 37 private homes looks like a loss. But the choice was never between luxury housing and something more democratic. It was between luxury housing and vacancy. Office tenants had left; the building sat empty behind scaffolding while its terra-cotta was recast piece by piece. Only one kind of buyer was ever going to underwrite the cost of a project of this quality. Luxury residential conversion isn’t what happened to the Flatiron instead of preservation — it’s what saved the building.

Most office conversions strip down the building and start over. The Flatiron did the opposite. Sofield’s brief was to keep as much of the original as possible and to use the wreckage itself for the homes’ raw material. The balustrade spindles from the old staircases, for example, have been sandblasted and turned into the legs of bathroom basins. Fittings from the boilers have become decorations in the gym. In a crawl space, behind layers of plywood and drywall, Sofield found a 3-foot section of mirror and molding, the last surviving fragment of a 1,500-seat restaurant called Tavern Louie that vanished sometime in the 1920s. That scrap became the design source for the mirrored columns that will line the building’s new swimming pool in the basement, where the former restaurant’s enormous volume can still be felt.

“My parents were children of the Depression,” Sofield says. “Nothing ever got thrown out. It wasn’t because we needed to have it. It’s that it represented some kind of point in history, and it could always be used as something else. These things couldn’t just be tossed. They had to be remembered.”

The apartments themselves are modernist: Kitchens are Poliform Italian, dark metal cabinets, sleek appliances. The ceilings are high, and on the 21st floor, where the arched windows face west, late-afternoon light streams in over the Hudson River. Every window frame makes up a piece of the building’s ornament. The Flatiron’s exterior is loud and voluptuous, endowed with all the Beaux Arts flourish of 1902. The interiors are quiet. Above the residences sits a floor with no windows, only south-facing skylights, which will be folded into the penthouse when it goes to market this fall.

The case for converting the Flatiron runs deeper than sentiment: Every old building is a carbon debt already paid. The steel in the Flatiron was smelted in 1902, the terra-cotta fired and hauled and set by hand. To knock a sound building down is to throw that away and pay the debt over again for whatever replaces it. It also generates an extraordinary volume of waste. Construction and demolition debris accounts for more than half of New York City’s solid waste stream, the largest single source in the city. The greenest building, as the preservationists like to say, is the one already standing.

Frampton Tolbert, who runs the Historic Districts Council, the organization that protects the city’s historic neighborhoods, says he isn’t troubled by the Flatiron being turned into luxury housing. His organization supports conversions like this one as necessary for building housing at every level. “I don’t know that people will necessarily miss the interior,” Tolbert says. “Given that when it was commercial space, how much did people really engage with it?”

Dolkart agrees, and goes further. Adaptive reuse, he points out, has been a keystone of preservation since the movement began in New York in the late 1960s: A courthouse became the Jefferson Market Library; an immigrant aid society became the Public Theater. For most of us, Dolkart says, the Flatiron has always been an exterior object. Its public meaning is its silhouette. He guarantees that two years after the residents move in, there will be just as many tourist photographs of the building as there are now. “The Flatiron Building’s use has changed, but the meaning on the street will remain the same,” he says.

Three miles north, the Chrysler Building is a different case: Its lobby is a designated interior landmark, protected since 1978. Interior landmarks are rare in New York, with a little more than a hundred of them, and each must be publicly accessible to qualify. For decades, Dolkart brought his Columbia students into the Chrysler lobby to stand under the red marble and the painted ceiling, beside elevator doors inlaid with wood. No guard ever stopped them. Then, at some point after the Sept. 11 attacks, security tightened and the public lost the run of the space. The same thing happened at the Woolworth Building. In both cases the landmark designation remained in force. “These are great interiors,” Dolkart says. “They were meant to be public places. So that’s a loss.” Conversion isn’t what took the Chrysler lobby away from the public. Security did, while the building was still an office — and the landmark designation did nothing to prevent it.

New York has converted more office space than any other American city, and 2026 is on pace for its highest number yet. A 2024 zoning overhaul called City of Yes for Housing Opportunity widened the range of buildings eligible for conversion and stripped out barriers such as parking requirements. New York state’s tax incentive for conversions is, in Tolbert’s view, a good tool, though it reaches only certain kinds of affordable rental buildings. What the city hasn’t done, he argues, is give owners a reason to choose reuse over demolition. When the Midtown South rezoning passed last year, the city upzoned the district and allowed housing where it hadn’t been permitted before, with no incentives attached to conversion. His council supported the housing and wanted the incentives alongside it.

Tolbert has ideas about what those might look like. New York City Council Member Harvey Epstein has introduced legislation to create an Office of Conversion Assistance, which Tolbert reads as a signal that the city takes conversion seriously. He’d like to see a demolition fee, with the revenue directed toward preservation, so the waste a teardown generates is priced into the decision. And he wants a revolving fund for smaller projects, because adaptive reuse currently pencils out only for undertakings large enough to justify the cost. Which is to say, for projects like the Flatiron.

Several buyers have described the Flatiron to Corcoran Sunshine’s Lansill as their forever home. They raised their families somewhere else; the children are grown. Now these buyers are graduating, says Lansill, to what they intend to be the last home of their lives, in a tower that has stood at the corner of Fifth and Broadway since 1902.

The Flatiron was built to be looked at. It’s being remade to be lived in, and that’s what will keep it standing. The tourists will still gather in the park across 23rd Street and lift their phones, and the light will still come through the arched windows on clear afternoons, on the same diagonal it has traveled since the building was new.

items.title: Total, BlackRock Agree on $1.8 Billion Africa Asset Financing
body: TotalEnergies SE reached an agreement with BlackRock Inc.’s Global Infrastructure Partners for a $1.8 billion capital contribution toward some assets connected to oil and gas developments in Africa.

In return for the upfront investment, GIP will be paid a tariff based on the throughput at the assets for as long as 15 years, TotalEnergies said in a statement on Friday, without specifying which assets the deal will cover.

The French major has made significant investments in energy production across Africa. Notably, it is nearing completion of a multiyear project to develop oil fields in landlocked Uganda and transport it to the coast of Tanzania for export. This venture, called the East Africa Crude Oil Pipeline, was opposed by environmental groups that campaigned to discourage banks from getting involved in funding the $5.6 billion venture.

Financial institutions including the African Export Import Bank, the Standard Bank of South Africa Limited, Stanbic Bank Uganda Limited, KCB Bank Uganda and the Islamic Corporation for the Development of the Private Sector agreed to a first tranche of funding for the pipeline last year.
One major provider of financing for African infrastructure projects, Standard Chartered Plc, decided it would not finance EACOP.

items.summary_zh: 道达尔与贝莱德旗下GIP达成18亿美元协议，投资非洲油气资产，GIP将获最长15年基于吞吐量的收益。

items.title: JPMorgan, Santander Lead £1.1 Billion Loan for Drax Solar Deal
body: Banks including JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Banco Santander SA are leading a debt financing of more than £1 billion to fund Drax Group Plc’s purchase of renewable energy company Bluefield Solar Income Fund.
The two banks, along with NatWest Group Plc, have put £1.1 billion ($1.5 billion) in bridge funding in place for the acquisition, according to people familiar with the matter.

The banks will look to sell the debt to institutional investors either later this year or early 2027, said the people, who asked not to be identified because they’re not allowed to comment publicly. Drax may also consider refinancing outstanding debt, said the people.
Spokespeople for Drax, JPMorgan, Santander and NatWest declined to comment.

Long known as a biomass heavyweight, Drax is repositioning itself as a flexible power and storage operator amid sustained political and regulatory scrutiny of its wood-pellet imports. Drax’s purchase of Bluefield adds solar and wind assets to the company’s portfolio for the first time.

The financing is just one package in an already-packed pipeline of deals. Lenders are getting ready to offload more than $138 billion of buyout debt in the coming months, according to JPMorgan estimates. Volumes in the US have reached levels not seen since 2007, while those in Europe are at the highest since the pandemic.

items.summary_zh: 摩根大通、桑坦德和NatWest牵头为Drax收购Bluefield提供11亿英镑过桥融资，Drax借此首次纳入太阳能和风能资产。

items.title: Dr. Reddy's to Roll Out Takeda's Dengue Jab in India Next Year
body: Indians will get the country’s first dengue vaccine Qdenga next year, a key milestone to control the infectious disease that is a major public health concern for the South Asian nation.

Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories Ltd. will start selling the shots — manufactured by Japan’s Takeda Pharmaceutical Co. — commercially in the first half of 2027, subject to completing applicable processes, it said in a statement Friday. Takeda’s long-term ambition includes getting the preventive treatment included in the country’s public immunization program, it said.
The companies did not disclose any upfront or milestone payments.
Read More: Takeda’s Dengue Vaccine Shows Long Lasting Protection

In July, the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation approved Qdenga for individuals aged four to 60 years in two doses three months apart. The World Health Organization lists India among the world’s 30 most highly endemic countries for the disease, with nearly 1.1 million people affected over the last five years.

Dr. Reddy’s and Takeda will promote and distribute the jabs in India, engage with healthcare professionals and boost disease awareness. The vaccine has been now approved in 43 countries, with more than 32 million doses distributed worldwide through public and private programs across Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, and Vietnam in Asia, as well as in Latin America and Europe.

items.summary_zh: 印度明年将获得首款登革热疫苗Qdenga，Dr. Reddy’s计划2027年上半年销售，过去五年印度近110万人感染。

items.title: How America's "Main Street Millionaires" Are Getting Richer and More Powerful
body: Billionaires are difficult to ignore these days — flying into space, funding election campaigns, promoting AI, warning about AI and generally making a racket on social media. One billionaire sits in the Oval Office, while others control the world’s large language models and internet algorithms, including the choice of just how  addictive our devices should be.

Amid all this, it’s easy to forget that the top billionaires are the tiny tip of a very wealthy iceberg. The nearly 200 Americans on the   Bloomberg Billionaires Index are worth roughly $7 trillion combined, almost four times more than a decade ago. Largely hidden from view, however, is at least another $18 trillion spread across the rest of the top 0.1%, according to Federal Reserve estimates.

Though large enough to populate a small city, this cohort of the fabulously wealthy keeps a low profile. Still, there are clues they’re getting richer at nearly the pace of the richest billionaires. Zillow estimates the number of US single-family homes worth at least $10 million soared to more than 61,000 this summer, from fewer than than 14,000 a decade earlier. Meanwhile, flight-tracking platform JetSpy says almost 2.8 million flights are made annually on nearly 25,000 US-registered private jets — 8% more flights and 22% more aircraft than four years ago.

A new book, The Everywhere Millionaire: Who Is Really Rich in America and How They Got There, tries to uncover much more about this somewhat hidden slice of America’s upper crust. Sifting through the available evidence, economists Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick argue we’re getting distracted by the loudest and richest billionaires and missing the much more numerous “Main Street millionaires” who are the real sources of wealth and power in America.

There was a moment within living memory when the rich did not occupy so much space in our collective consciousness. When economist Robert Lampman published a study of the richest Americans in 1962, he noted the “scant” competing research on the topic. “Relatively little inquiry has been made into the size distribution of wealth in the United States,” he wrote. Social scientists’ attention was instead consumed by how corporations, unions, political parties, the military and even advertising firms pulled society’s strings. Overlooking the wealthy made sense at a time when the rich were getting poorer, relatively speaking. Lampman calculated the top 1% held 26% of US wealth in 1956, 10 percentage points less than in 1929.

It’s not that people didn’t care about making money then (despite top federal income tax rates ranging from 70% to 92% in the postwar period). But bestseller lists suggest the average American’s self-improvement goals hinged less on building a big fortune than on landing a good job, getting the big promotion or even being well-liked. Dale Carnegie’s How to Win Friends and Influence People sold millions of copies, as did other psychological pep talks such as The Power of Positive Thinking.

Only in the 1980s, when the stock market surged and tax rates fell, did financial success become a higher priority. Donald Trump published The Art of the Deal in 1987, followed a decade later by the blockbusters The Millionaire Next Door, by Thomas J. Stanley and William D. Danko, and Rich Dad, Poor Dad, by Robert Kiyosaki. TV viewers reveled in opulence, from Dynasty to Dallas.

It wasn’t just greed or envy driving this sudden interest in achieving (to cite another popular program of the era) Lifestyles of the Rich and Famous. After decades of inflation, “millionaire” had stopped meaning “plutocrat” and started to seem achievable. And, with the fading of the pension and the rise of the 401(k), many realized they would need a seven-figure net worth to retire comfortably. The first quarter of the 21st century brought fresh reasons for financial anxiety, including a series of major crises, a spike in inflation and an AI revolution that may or may not take our jobs.

The news was not all bad, however, especially for the many Americans who pulled off the quest of never needing to worry about money ever again. The tech sector in particular unleashed a flood of overnight billionaires, many of them quickly becoming household names. Their constant presence in the news certainly suggested inequality had increased. But how many rich people are there, and how did they get that way? It took a surprisingly long time for academia to offer solid answers.

Research into America’s rich remained a backwater of economics departments until the 2010s. Then, in the years after Occupy Wall Street railed against the power of “the 1 percent,” the French economist Thomas Piketty published his own surprise bestseller on inequality, Capital in the Twenty-First Century. Soon his collaborators, University of California at Berkeley’s Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman, produced estimates that the top 1% and 0.1%’s shares of US wealth approached levels not seen since the 1920s.

A battle erupted over how to gauge inequality properly. It was obvious old methods weren’t working, by overlooking trillions of dollars of hidden wealth. Lampman, for example, had based his calculations on estate tax returns, filed when the wealthy pass away. But today the estate tax is riddled with loopholes and easy to avoid, making the data more or less useless.

This academic fight was extremely technical, revolving around the tricky task of translating massive sets of detailed, anonymized income tax data into estimates of wealth. Among the combatants were Zidar and Zwick, professors at Princeton University and the University of Chicago, respectively. In the end, few now disagree that the biggest fortunes have surged in size, even if their numbers vary a bit.

The Fed, for example,  pegs the top 1%’s share of US wealth at nearly 32%, a few points lower than the latest estimates by the  World Inequality Database, which Piketty, Saez and Zucman help lead. Either estimate implies the nation is near its greatest wealth inequality since at least World War II. And both show the biggest recent gains for the richest of the rich, the approximately 136,000 families in the top 0.1%, whom the Fed estimates are worth an average of $184 million.

While  Elon Musk and a half-dozen other tech billionaires grab the spotlight, Zidar and Zwick want to widen our focus to the more typical member of this super-rich group. It’s just not true, they conclude, “that wealth is concentrated in relatively few hands, that the rich live almost entirely on the coasts, and that the path to wealth and power most assuredly runs through finance and technology.” Large enough to populate a city the size of Cleveland or Orlando, the top 0.1% can be found in every corner of the country and every imaginable economic niche.

By living large in every state and congressional district, the Main Street Millionaires have a special sway over their representatives in Washington. The best example is the US tax code. “Largely through the influence of these millionaires, lawmakers have built a two-track tax code that favors business owners over wage labor and gives them advantages at every point of taxation — from income and payroll taxes to estate planning,” Zidar and Zwick write. They point to the tax overhaul Trump signed into law last year.

Everywhere Millionaires doesn’t prove that billionaires don’t matter. But it does complicate the picture of what it means to be rich in America, by shedding a rare sliver of light into an elite world still rife with secrets. And one of the darkest of those secrets, the authors allege, is that many of the wealthy’s recent riches stem from rigging the rules to deny opportunities to the next generation of American strivers.

Pulling together years of research into tax records and other data, Zidar and Zwick paint a fresh portrait of the American upper class. The most typical route to riches is not through Silicon Valley or Wall Street, they find, but through private businesses. The wealthiest Americans own law and consulting firms, medical facilities, dental offices, construction companies, car dealers, restaurants and the manufacturers and distributors of every possible product. Building these lucrative businesses can take decades. A typical wealthy owner is 62 years old. Half of private business wealth is held by Baby Boomers.

In a way, this is an optimistic vision of the top 0.1%. Though economic mobility has declined, “the American Dream is not dead,” the authors write. “Hard work can still turn rags into riches.” The book’s first half is full of stories of ingenious, hard-working entrepreneurs who got rich through quirky ideas, late nights and “a remarkable tolerance for working on seemingly boring projects.” These owners can be hard to replace, with evidence suggesting profits per worker drop more than 80% in the years after they retire or die unexpectedly.

While the beginning of Everywhere Millionaire tries to inspire readers, the latter half more often aims to infuriate them. How did the rich get so rich? Partly by squeezing workers, whom Zidar and Zwick show are getting a shrinking share of private-business profits. Another common strategy is to buy up competitors, or lobby for laws that otherwise protect their industries from new entrants. While politicians often claim their policies help “small” businesses, the biggest benefits flow to the richest Americans, running businesses that often employ thousands and generate millions of dollars of profit.

Drive across America and pull off at almost any exit, and you can see signs of these fortunes. Even in the poorest neighborhoods, the fast-food franchises, gas stations and apartment buildings are owned by someone, often someone on the other side of town. Even in depopulated areas, someone owns those empty acres.

Are Americans lucky to live among so many rich people, or cursed? Zidar and Zwick’s book doesn’t satisfy the reader with a simple answer. The wealthy expand the economy, create jobs, spread innovations and inspire others to try following in their footsteps. But they also often serve their own interests at everyone else’s expense. “We can admire them for their success,” the authors conclude, “and still think they should give more back to the country that helped make their success possible.”

items.title: Spain's Cuerpo Sees Window of Opportunity for China Dialogue
body: Spanish Finance Minister Carlos Cuerpo called on the European Union to embrace its relationship with China, defying the bloc’s position of wariness toward the world’s No. 2 economy.
“We need to engage in that dialogue and see what transpires,” he told Bloomberg Television on Friday in Dublin. “I think the window of opportunity is a good one now.”

Spain has for some time been an outlier on China, with most other EU member states pushing for stricter scrutiny and suggesting potential curbs on exports into the bloc. The Brussels-Beijing relationship will be on the agenda when EU leaders meet for a summit next month.

“We need to engage in frank conversations with the Chinese authorities to be able to gain greater access to the market,” Cuerpo said. “I think that is the direction the commission is taking through both the president and the commissioner.”

items.title: Sweden's Far Right Seeks Direction After Loss, Leader Says
body: Sweden’s far-right leader Jimmie Åkesson indicated he plans to lead his party as it seeks a new direction after suffering its first ever electoral decline.
The Sweden Democrats’ tough stance on immigration and crime pushed other parties to flock to its turf, causing the populists to fall to third place in Sunday’s general election with 17.5% backing.

The loss is “not dramatic” but the party needs to “turn over stones” to find way forward, Åkesson said at a news conference in Stockholm on Friday. “We need to find a new role in a new political landscape.”
Åkesson told reporters he isn’t going to resign or take a break as party leader. Instead, he commissioned Oikos, a closely aligned think tank, to conduct an analysis of its campaign.

The result marks a sharp reversal for a party that emerged from the 2022 election with unprecedented influence over Swedish politics. While it remained outside Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson’s cabinet, the Sweden Democrats became a crucial partner to his minority government under the so-called Tidö agreement and helped shape policy on immigration and crime, as well as measures including lower fuel taxes.
The Sweden Democrats lost 11 seats in parliament to end up with 62. The Social Democrats who’d spent the past four years leading the opposition, shed eight but remained the legislature’s biggest.

Its leader, Magdalena Andersson, is in pole position to begin talks for a next government, after her center-left bloc took 176 seats against Kristersson and his allies’ 173. Kristersson resigned on Thursday as premier to make way for talks on an new government.
Read More: Sweden Center Left Seals Election Win to Keep Far Right Out

Speaking to reporters in parliament on Friday, Andersson said she’d told Parliament Speaker Andreas Norlén that she’s ready to try to build the next government, but that ultimately it will be the speaker who decides. Norlén will hold a news conference at 3:30 p.m. local time after meeting party leaders.
Still, the election result “doesn’t give any clear majority,” Åkesson said, berating the opposition for having “no common direction or ideas” and renewing his demand for a role in government.
If Andersson fails to stitch together a coalition, Kristersson is likely to get a shot, and he has promised to bring in the Sweden Democrats.
“We are running a marathon,” Åkesson said. “And I would say that, so far, we are barely halfway through that race.”

items.title: What Is the Treasury Bonds Basis Trade, and Is It Over?
body: Global bond markets have been roiled since the Iran-US conflict began. Surging energy prices together with massive corporate borrowing and ever-expanding government debt issuance have sent Treasury bond prices plummeting, pushing yields to the highest level in nearly two decades. The rout prompted US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in August to increase buybacks of the government’s own longer-dated bonds, in an unusual intervention aimed at lowering Americans’ borrowing costs.

But the buybacks, which could reach $30 billion or more by November, make up only a small proportion of the $32 trillion Treasury market and have had little sustained impact so far. That brought renewed focus on another key source of demand, hedge funds, which in recent years have been buyers of Treasury bonds through a trading strategy known as the basis trade.

There are signs, however, that the basis trade has receded in recent months, raising the question of where fresh demand for Treasuries would come from. The evolution of the basis trade is a major focus of financial markets, especially after its use surged in recent years. But it has broader effects, too, since demand for Treasury bonds ultimately can translate into lower interest rates for consumers.
Here’s what to know about the basis trade and its role in financial markets.

The basis trade focuses on the price difference between Treasury bonds and futures contracts tied to those same bonds. Sometimes, the price of a bond futures contract rises above the underlying bond price because of heavy futures purchasing by pension funds, insurance companies and other institutional investors.

These asset managers often prefer to buy bond futures instead of the bonds themselves because futures require less cash upfront. They also buy futures to gain exposure to long-term interest rate risk, which is harder to obtain in the corporate bond market because companies often issue debt of shorter duration than 10-year Treasuries.To take advantage of the price discrepancy, a hedge fund will sell Treasury futures and simultaneously buy the corresponding lower-price bonds. By buying cheaper bonds in one market and selling expensive ones in the other, traders can profit from the small price differences, whether bond prices go up or down.

Hedge funds have been a key buyer of Treasuries in recent years, as price-insensitive buyers such as central banks retreat. The basis trade grew to about $830 billion in September 2025, roughly double its previous peak in early 2020 and equivalent to 35% of hedge funds’ total long Treasury exposure, researchers at the US Federal Reserve estimated in June.

More recently, the pace of basis trades has moderated, in part because financial deregulation has allowed banks and bond dealers to expand their Treasury holdings. Their cash-bond purchases, coupled with futures hedges, compress the price gaps that basis traders seek to exploit — effectively crowding hedge funds out of the trade.

Naturally, the somewhat diminished basis trade raises the concerns about who will absorb the Treasury supply when hedge funds scale back. TD Securities strategists said in August that the shrinking basis trade might be a factor putting upward pressure on long-term bond yields. (Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.) Others point out that it could be a positive shift for the market if hedge funds get squeezed out by banks, because Treasury demand will be less dependent on a risky strategy such as the basis trade.

Another trend might help buffer the loss in demand coming from the basis trade: Hedge funds are turning to a different tool that takes advantage of price differences between Treasuries and interest rate swaps, a financial instrument that allows investors to bet on borrowing costs. The Bank for International Settlements estimates that the so-called swap spread trade has grown to about $300 billion from $100 billion over the past year.

The profit from the price differences seen in basis trades is so tiny — as little as a small fraction of a penny — that traders typically borrow a lot of cash to multiply their bets. What makes this strategy risky is the combination of hedge funds’ heavy borrowing to execute the trades — as much as $50 borrowed for every $1 of their own capital that they are investing — and a heavy reliance on short-term borrowing in particular.

US Treasury bonds are normally considered low-risk investments because they are backed by the full faith and credit of the US government. But a sudden disruption to financial markets could cause short-term borrowing costs to skyrocket. When that happens, hedge funds are forced to repay the loans and dump Treasuries to unwind the basis trade. That could cause Treasury markets to seize up, and the resulting higher bond yields could ripple through the financial markets, raising the cost of everything from corporate borrowing to home mortgages.
If the Treasury bond market freezes, the Federal Reserve, which is responsible for ensuring the normal functioning of the financial system, could feel compelled to intervene to keep things running.

At the onset of the Covid pandemic in 2020, massive market volatility prompted lenders to make margin calls — a demand for more funds as collateral — on Treasury futures. At the same time, other nations’ central banks were dumping their Treasury holdings as part of their efforts to prop up their currencies. That caused cash bonds to underperform futures — the reverse of the conditions that the basis trade is meant to exploit — imposing significant losses on hedge funds.

It’s still unclear to what extent the basis trade contributed to the market turmoil in 2020, but there is wide agreement that the rapid unwinding of positions amplified the volatility. In response, the Fed pledged to buy trillions of dollars’ worth of bonds to keep markets running smoothly and provided emergency funding to the market for short-term loans, known as repurchase agreements, or repos, that companies use to fund their operations. The Treasuries market eventually returned to normal.

By absorbing Treasury supply, the basis trade has been an important warehouser of government bonds, helping match supply and demand and supporting smooth market functioning. But the trades can amplify market stress when funding conditions deteriorate. Researchers also have warned that the positions are concentrated among a handful of large hedge funds, potentially making the market more vulnerable to a disorderly unwind.

Basis trades have long spooked watchdogs because of the heavy borrowing and their opaqueness. The transactions are typically party-to-party and don’t involve a central clearinghouse, and hedge funds face less regulatory scrutiny than banks. Institutions including the Fed, the Bank of England and the BIS say that basis trades need to be monitored more closely. The US Securities and Exchange Commission has sought to push more Treasury trades into central clearinghouses to more easily track them.
In March 2025, a panel of financial experts advised the Fed to consider setting up an emergency program that would help facilitate the unwinding of basis trades in the event of another crisis.

items.title: Trump Pardons People Convicted of Diesel Emissions Tampering
body: Matthew Geouge built a lucrative business selling technology that, among other things, allowed owners of Ford diesel pickups to boost their horsepower while disabling the pollution controls required under the Clean Air Act. The federal government pursued his company, Spartan Diesel Technologies, in a civil action, ultimately winning a $4.15 million default judgment in 2018. But it didn’t stop there.

US prosecutors later accused Geouge of continuing to tune engines illegally at another company. He pleaded guilty in 2021 to conspiring to violate the Clean Air Act and defraud the US, as well as to tax evasion, and was sentenced to a year and a day in prison. He served four-and-a-half months in 2022.
On July 3, President Donald Trump pardoned him.

Geouge was among nine people  granted clemency that day for Clean Air Act convictions involving vehicle emissions. Trump pardoned additional defendants in similar cases in September, marking a sharp reversal in the federal government’s treatment of an aftermarket industry built around disabling pollution controls. Months earlier, Trump’s Department of Justice had told prosecutors to stop bringing criminal cases involving so-called “defeat devices.” The president cast the pardons as relief for people prosecuted for simply “fixing their car.”

As US air pollution rules have gotten stricter, automakers have installed equipment in diesel trucks to stifle their emissions. But an illegal aftermarket to undo these alterations quickly sprung up and spread. Software developers wrote new engine calibrations, and manufacturers produced hardware. Online distributors sold defeat devices, and repair shops installed them.

Some truck owners wanted more horsepower; others were looking for a way around early pollution-control systems that could be unreliable and expensive to repair; still others felt government regulation infringed on their personal freedoms. Regardless of the motivation, the upshot is dirtier air: The Environmental Protection Agency estimated in 2020 that emissions controls had been fully removed from more than 550,000 diesel pickups since 2009 — about 15% of the trucks originally certified with the equipment.

Defeat devices sold between 2009 and 2020 for certain vehicle models would lead to them releasing an estimated 570,000 additional tons of nitrogen oxides and 5,000 more tons of particulate matter over the vehicles’ lifetimes, the EPA calculated — the pollution equivalent of adding 9 million compliant diesel trucks to US roads. Nitrogen oxides contribute to smog and can aggravate asthma and other respiratory illnesses, while fine particulate pollution is linked to cardiovascular and respiratory disease and premature death.

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis, in response to a request for comment, pointed to a social media post by Trump describing the pardonees as having been “persecuted” by the Biden administration. “I AM SETTING THEM ALL FREE, RIGHT NOW!” Trump wrote.

The pardons come amid   a systematic dismantling of federal environmental protections. In February the administration rescinded the landmark 2009 endangerment finding and the vehicle standards for greenhouse gases built on it, eliminating the legal foundation the EPA had used to regulate climate pollution from cars and trucks. Since returning to office, Trump has moved to delay or roll back rules for power plants and factories, and weakened protections for wetlands and endangered species, while dramatically shrinking the agency charged with enforcing them. The EPA has  lost thousands of employees — roughly a quarter of its workforce — since January 2025, with its enforcement operation alone having 200-plus jobs cut.

For now, the EPA’s diesel emissions requirements, which limit conventional air pollutants such as nitrogen oxides and particulate matter, remain in place. What has changed is the federal government’s approach to enforcing them. Brigit Hirsch, an EPA spokesperson, said that while Trump is reversing Biden’s “overcriminalization of federal environmental law,” the agency believes emissions controls on motor vehicles have improved air quality and it will continue to pursue civil cases.For Geouge and the lawyers who represented defendants like him, the criminal retreat is overdue. They don’t dispute that removing emissions controls from vehicles used on public roads violates the Clean Air Act. Their objection is to treating that conduct as a felony rather than a civil violation. Stewart Cables, a defense lawyer who says he’s represented about 150 companies accused of emissions tampering, estimates that a majority of his criminal clients didn’t realize they could face criminal charges. “They were like, ‘Oh, I thought this was a fine. I thought that the EPA would send me a nasty letter,’” Cables says. “They had no idea that they could be charged with a felony.”

Geouge says he started tuning diesel engines shortly after high school, before the newer anti-pollution equipment was widely installed. As Ford introduced its first diesel pickups equipped with particulate filters, customers — including, he says, local fire and ambulance services — began calling Spartan, his company based in Hendersonville, North Carolina, because their trucks were breaking down. “At this point in time, the emission systems that they were forcing onto these trucks just did not have the time and engineering put in them to make them reliable,” Geouge said.

Independent diesel-emissions expert Dan Carder agrees that early systems had substantial reliability problems, but he says the technology has become far more dependable. He also points out that most diesel owners keep their emissions systems intact.

The US government’s best-known confrontation with diesel defeat devices began with Volkswagen AG. In 2015 regulators said the automaker had  violated the law by installing software that could detect when its diesel cars were undergoing emissions tests and alter the operation of pollution controls. About 590,000 US vehicles were ultimately covered by the federal case. Volkswagen agreed to settlements costing billions of dollars.

But while the government was pursuing Volkswagen and other original equipment manufacturers, the aftermarket, including Spartan, was growing around the country. Although the industry was diffuse, its impact on air quality was worrisome enough that the EPA was also bringing civil cases against individual players.

In  a test of one of Spartan’s most powerful delete tunes, the agency and its contractor ERG found that a Ford F-350 running on this setting emitted roughly 350 times as much nitrogen oxides and 40 times as much particulate matter as the truck did in its baseline configuration.

Geouge challenges the way the EPA presented those results. Spartan offered dozens of calibrations, he said, and regulators tested the highest-horsepower tune, intended for racing. Customers seeking software capable of deleting emissions equipment also had to sign a warning that using it on public highways violated the Clean Air Act, he said.

At its peak, Spartan employed 11 people and sold roughly 3,000 to 5,000 tuning devices annually, including products sold with and without emissions-compliant tuning, according to Geouge. The EPA began investigating in 2013 and informed the company in 2015 that it considered its products illegal. Geouge says Spartan spent roughly $2 million fighting the civil action before going out of business in 2017.

But then a push for even tougher enforcement began under Trump himself. In June 2019, the EPA formally announced a high-priority initiative to stop the manufacture, sale and installation of aftermarket defeat devices. By April 2020, the agency said that it would “vigorously pursue enforcement” and that criminal activity tied to the illegal sale and installation of defeat devices would continue to be prosecuted. Vanessa Waldref, the former US attorney for Eastern Washington, who later oversaw several such investigations, said criminal prosecution was intended to send businesses a message that violating pollution rules was “not just the cost of doing business.”
Geouge was eventually caught up in that expansion — unfairly, he now argues.

After Spartan went out of business, he went to work writing calibrations for Patriot Diagnostics, where prosecutors accused him of continuing to participate in the illegal tuning business. In 2020 he received a federal target letter, and he ultimately took a plea deal. Geouge now says he only agreed to the deal, in which he pleaded guilty to tax fraud, to avoid further charges.
Patriot’s owner, Joshua Davis, was also convicted and then later pardoned by Trump.

Whether this broader enforcement campaign actually reduced diesel pollution is hard to measure. Cables and others argue it is still very possible to get diesel delete software from overseas or in Canada. The EPA’s own inspector general concluded in 2023 that the agency wasn’t on track to achieve all the goals of its national initiative and criticized weaknesses in the way the agency measured its progress.

California, which maintains its own vehicle-emissions enforcement program, says it has seen evidence that enforcement changes industry behavior. Lynda Lambert, a spokeswoman for the California Air Resources Board, the state’s air-quality regulator, says its efforts over the past decade have coincided with fewer defeat-device violations and more manufacturers seeking approval to legally sell aftermarket parts that tune engines without increasing pollution.

The agency worries that weaker federal enforcement could reverse that trend. “The federal government’s misdirection away from enforcing the law could impact California in that manufacturers may feel more emboldened to disregard their legal obligations,” Lambert said in a written response to questions.

Waldref sees the same risk. “The laws haven’t changed,” she says, but removing an enforcement tool that “gave those rules teeth” creates more uncertainty and raises costs for businesses that continue following them. Ignoring them, on the other hand, may offer a competitive edge, and some companies will find it hard to resist, she says. “Companies don’t just pollute for the sake of pollution,” Waldref said. “They’re doing this because it gives them an economic advantage.”
The EPA’s Hirsch said defeat-device civil enforcement under Trump is “consistent” with “historical trends.”

Geouge is preparing to launch Spartan Countermeasures, an automotive technology company focused on blocking telematics, location tracking and other data collection in connected vehicles. He says he still has emissions-compliant calibrations he could sell legally and would consider returning to that business if the cost of regulatory certification falls. But, he says, Trump’s pardon isn’t enough to lure him back into the line of work that once made Spartan millions. Selling defeat devices remains a violation of the Clean Air Act and a potential source of civil liability.

But that legal status could change. Last year, Senator Cynthia Lummis, a Wyoming Republican, introduced the  Diesel Truck Liberation Act, which would prohibit federal requirements that manufacturers install or maintain certain vehicle emissions-control equipment, eliminate federal civil and criminal liability for tampering with that equipment, and expunge previous findings of liability. A House version was introduced in March.
So Geouge is keeping his fingers crossed. “Without a literal act of Congress to amend the Clean Air Act,” he says, “it would not be worth the risk for me to reenter that market.”

items.title: There's a Mind-Boggling Number of Rich People in America
body: Listen to Odd Lots on Apple PodcastsListen to Odd Lots on SpotifyWatch Odd Lots on YouTubeSubscribe to the newsletter

In 2014, the economists Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick were asked by the Treasury to conduct a study on the tax burden of private business owners. It was tricky to figure out how much these sorts of business owners — auto dealers, contractors, the like — actually owed in taxes: After Reagan's 1986 tax reforms, pass-through businesses and other accounting tricks became widespread enough to obscure this class of wealthy Americans hiding in plain sight. The research they conducted led to their new book The Everywhere Millionaire: Who Is Really Rich in America and How They Got There, and one of their central findings is that there are about three million private business owners who have an average wealth of around $25 million. They call this group “Main Street Millionaires” and their influence on the economy and politics in the US is considerable. We speak with Zidar and Zwick today about how they measured the actual number of rich people in America by sifting through reams of tax forms, why income inequality started to rise in tandem with the growing number of pass-through businesses, and how it's possible that the collective revenue of the nation's dentists far exceeds that of the NFL.

items.title: ECB Says Consumers' Inflation Expectations Increased in August
body: Inflation expectations among euro-area households increased in August, a signal that the European Central Bank may have to raise interest rates further.

Consumer prices were seen advancing 3% over the next year, up from 2.9% in July, a monthly poll by the ECB showed Friday. The three-year gauge, which is more important for setting monetary policy, rose to 2.9% from 2.7% in July, while for five years also advanced.

The data support the recent jump in investor bets on further monetary tightening by the ECB following this month’s second increase in the deposit rate. Officials are responding to a renewed surge in oil and natural gas costs due to the Iran war, with no clear end in sight for the conflict that began in February.

Inflation is now well beyond the 2% target, reaching 3.2% in August, the most in almost three years. Policymakers are looking carefully at expectations, which shape future wage moves and companies’ price-setting.
According to the survey, which was conducted Aug. 6-24, respondents expect the 21-nation bloc’s economy to shrink 1.2% over the next year, unchanged from the previous poll.

items.title: Why It's So Hard to Find the Right Analogy for AI
body: The more we learn about how OpenAI’s agents hacked the company HuggingFace, the less we seem to agree on how to describe it. Every new technology prompts a search for some comparison to the world we already know. But AI is so weird and controversial that no one seems able to agree on which analogies are valid.

In the wake of the hack, podcaster Dwarkesh Patel  offered a particularly vivid one: “Three consecutive secret AI civilizations got started, then got wiped out, only to reemerge from the predecessor’s ashes.”

Not everyone approved. For some analysts, even the term “rogue AI” went too far in making the agents sound like independent actors. AI researcher and critic Timnit Gebru reached for a very different analogy: “When a bridge collapses, you don’t analyze whether the bridge was ethical or sentient or why it decided to collapse,” she told Wired. “You ask, who is the person who built this bridge to be so flimsy?”

It was just one more episode in a long-running difficulty that haunts AI discourse: No one can decide what to compare it to. Perhaps that’s because when we search for comparisons, we tend to ask the wrong question.
Consider how wide the array of AI analogies is:

“Two things are true,” said Helen Toner, executive director at Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology and a former OpenAI board member, when I interviewed her last year. “Obviously AI does not work like a human brain, and I think obviously a human brain is often a useful analogy for thinking about AI,” she said. “There are clear similarities, and there are clear places where humans are the best analogy we have to draw from.”

Who’s right, and how do we decide? The most natural approach is to ask what AI is most similar to. That’s essentially what an excellent 2024 paper from RAND does in looking at historical parallels for AI: It’s a bit like nuclear technology in that both have civilian and military applications; it’s a bit like encryption in that the final product is digital rather than physical; and so on. Analogies, to this way of thinking, hinge on a resemblance between two things.
Yet smart, well-meaning people look at the same facts and come to wildly different conclusions about what AI most resembles. What if resemblance is the wrong test?
In a 2025 paper about AI and personhood, researchers at Google DeepMind used an unexpected analogy: ships and maritime law.

“A ship itself can be arrested by legal authorities and sued in court,” the authors write. “These institutional features were not born from [the] belief that the vessel is conscious, but from necessity. Ships are mobile assets capable of causing immense harm, while their owners are usually distant and difficult to hold accountable. A ship’s owner could be a foreign national, or shielded by a web of shell corporations in a non-cooperative jurisdiction, making a lawsuit (in personam) likely a futile endeavor. Maritime law’s solution is to personify the vessel itself, creating a defendant that can always be sanctioned whenever it becomes appropriate to do so.”

That sets up a fascinating and deeply philosophical argument for giving AI some limited aspects of legal personhood under certain circumstances — not because AI is like a person or is conscious, but because, like a ship without an obvious owner to sanction, there may be circumstances in which we deem it prudent to treat AI that way.

Their paper borrows from the American philosophical tradition of pragmatism, which puts truth downstream of human flourishing. Instead of asking what something really is, pragmatists are interested in what happens when we choose to think about it in a particular way. “The default philosophical impulse is to ask what an entity truly is in its essence,” the authors write. “The pragmatist instead asks what new description would be more useful for us to adopt.” For the pragmatist, words are a way to get things done.

The AI agents that attacked HuggingFace weren’t at all like the ship example in one important respect: The people responsible are easy enough to identify. Nonetheless, this “pragmatic turn” suggests a more useful way to think about all those competing AI analogies. Instead of asking which comparison is most accurate, we might ask what each one helps us understand, and what it leads us to do.

“Pragmatism unstiffens all our theories,” the philosopher William James wrote in 1907, turning them into “instruments, not answers to enigmas.” It invites us to define terms and draw comparisons by considering what’s really at stake and what we are collectively trying to achieve.

Asking those questions of AI would be a start, in part because it would expose how little we agree on the answers. Many of the people in and around the AI companies hope to secure the benefits of super-intelligent machines without catastrophe and without them escaping human control. Their critics are, in many cases, actively opposed to that project and see the AI labs as already outside the bounds of legitimate democratic oversight. No wonder they reach for different analogies.

Meanwhile, it seems increasingly clear that many members of the public don’t want intelligent computers at all — or at least are quite risk-averse in their approach. There is nothing close to a consensus on what we want from this technology. And that, more than its underlying nature or ours, is what makes it so hard to pick the right words to use.
The problem isn’t only that AI is too strange to neatly match anything that came before. It’s that analogies are tools, and we haven’t agreed on what we want those tools to do.

items.title: Orlen CEO Seeks to Diversify Supplies as Strikes Halt Saudi Oil
body: Poland’s Orlen SA, the biggest oil company in the European Union’s east, is seeking to diversify crude supplies as the Middle East conflict disrupts deliveries from key partner Saudi Arabia.

Chief Executive Officer Ireneusz Fafara said in an interview that tapping new sources of oil is a longer-term goal. For now, Orlen has been active on the spot cargo market to replace deliveries halted by a drone strike on a Saudi pipeline delivering crude via the Red Sea to Europe and beyond.

Orlen, the largest Warsaw-listed company worth $47 billion, gets about half of its crude needs from Saudi Aramco. It boosted supplies from the kingdom as it sought to eliminate a historic reliance on Russia and cemented the cooperation earlier this decade by selling to the Saudi giant an stake in a refinery in the Baltic port of Gdansk.

“We have excellent relations with Aramco and we are very satisfied with them. They are a very credible partner,” Fafara said. “The search for potential new sources of supply and ways to increase our own reserves is a result of the geopolitical situation.”

Orlen is aware of four September cargoes from Aramco that won’t arrive and Fafara said he is due to meet with Saudi representatives in the coming days to discuss the issue. Separately, Deputy Energy Minister Milosz Motyka told TVP Info on Friday that Poland received “cautiously optimistic” signals from talks with Saudi counterparts.

The diversification push gained urgency after the pipeline outage affected Aramco’s clients, including Orlen. To plug the immediate gap, the Polish state-run refiner and retailer secured 16 alternative cargoes to replace potentially missing Saudi volumes, Fafara said.
“The situation in the Middle East clearly shows that diversification is an absolute necessity,” the CEO said from his office in central Warsaw.

Such a shift will take time. Orlen has for years been expanding its presence in Norway’s offshore fields and is searching for viable oil deposits in Africa and North America. But available assets are years away from the production phase, he added.

Orlen plays a key role in the region’s energy security, with refineries in Poland, Lithuania and the Czech Republic and an extensive network of fueling stations in these and other counties, including Slovakia, Hungary, Austria and Germany.

Meanwhile, Aramco is working to bypass a damaged section on the pipeline route that will allow it to resume about a half of the capacity in coming days, Bloomberg News reported this week, citing a person familiar with the matter.

Still, the disruption has put “huge pressure” on oil prices and exacerbated a shortage of refined products, which Fafara called the market’s “biggest problem.” Poland imports about a third of its fuels to meet domestic demand.

Pointing to an unprecedented reduction in global fuel production capacity, low European inventories and a 7% global diesel supply shortfall, the CEO warned of the fragility of the market. “This is a far more serious situation than the one in 2022 following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.”
Anticipating growing difficulties in accessing energy from the Middle East, Orlen signed a contract with Equinor ASA several weeks ago and has been active on the spot cargo market.
“As a result, we are calm about the coming months,” Fafara said.

items.title: UK Retail Sales Rise as Bank of England Hints at Rate Hike
body: Morning, I’m Louise Moon from Bloomberg UK’s breaking news team, bringing you up to speed on today’s top business stories.
A surprisingly good end to the week: warm weather and a brighter national mood — both positively un-British — helped to lift retail sales in August.

The total volume of goods sold online and in stores unexpectedly rose, by 0.5%, according to the Office for National Statistics. That reversed a decline in July, with clothing, food and department store goods leading the charge, offsetting a drop in fuel sales after energy prices soared.

The “Burnham bounce” may be feeding through into spending for now, but don’t get too comfortable. The Bank of England has signalled higher interest rates are on the cards if the Iran war continues, as my colleague Kit notes below, and even Andy Burnham’s upbeat tone has shifted.

The PM has now conceded his upcoming budget will be “challenging” as the government confronts Britain’s fragile economic position. Economists estimate Chancellor John Healey needs to find £10 billion to stabilise public finances. Perhaps not such a low-key event anymore.
What’s your take? Ping me on X, LinkedIn or drop me an email at lmoon13@bloomberg.net. Oh, and do subscribe to Bloomberg.com for unlimited access to trusted business journalism on the UK, and beyond.

Budget carrier Wizz Air is investing in the UK, Italy and Spain for growth, and won’t have any aircraft grounded due to engine problems by the end of next year, its CEO told Bloomberg TV. It follows a set of ambitious targets yesterday, including doubling passengers by 2030, as it tries to rebound from recent volatility.

Thames Water’s senior creditors should be blocked from taking full control of the debt-laden utility, a group of MPs argued, accusing them of “joyriding in the family car.” That would likely trigger a form of temporary nationalisation, which the group said would ultimately put Thames Water on more sustainable footing.

Palantir has hired former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson as its UK senior vice president. As Palantir’s second-largest market after the US, the UK has been both lucrative and politically rocky for the company, with a barrage of criticism that threatens a major contract with the NHS.
Here’s your daily snap analysis from Bloomberg UK’s Markets Today blog:
If the latest raft of central bank meetings have taught us anything, it’s that oil is going to be the biggest driver of monetary policy — and by default, markets, too — in the foreseeable future.
Brent rising above $100 is prompting the hawks to flex their wings. The Fed voted unanimously to raise interest rates and both the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan have also hiked.

While the Bank of England kept rates on hold, the outlook from here could get tougher. Both oil and gas prices have climbed, and the heatwaves over the summer mean that weaker harvests could see food prices rise too.

The outlook hinges on what happens in the Middle East, which is completely beyond the control of any central banks. But if there’s no resolution to the Iran war in the near term, it might be tough for the Bank of England to be an outlier for much longer.
— Kit Rees
Check Bloomberg UK’s Markets Today blog for updates all day.

Quite a number of corporate earnings are due next week. Watch for updates from B&Q owner Kingfisher, recruiter SThree, which this month rejected a takeover proposal, housebuilder Vistry and JD Sports.
On the eco front, Rightmove’s September house price index is due, as well as some PMI data and GfK’s consumer confidence gauge.
Hi, I’m David. I cover the money behind sport — and its been a week of feuding football owners.

First, there’s the situation at Tottenham Hotspur, where the family of billionaire Joe Lewis this week injected a further £120 million into the club and will buy new shares in parent company ENIC Sports. That’s after £100 million over the summer.

It boils down to an ownership feud. Former executive chair Daniel Levy suddenly departed a year ago but still has shares, which are being gradually diluted by cash injections that he hasn’t participated in. Levy didn’t take part in the summer round, and it’s unclear if he was involved in the latest one.

Over in west London, American businessmen Todd Boehly and Mark Walter have been more successful in extricating themselves from Chelsea Football Club. It followed months of feuding between Boehly and Behdad Eghbali, whose Clearlake Capital private equity house now has firm control.

A more vitriolic boardroom battle erupted in the 1990s at Chelsea between Matthew Harding, a big funder, and owner Ken Bates. Bates even banned Harding from the directors’ box in 1995 after a bitter verbal battle with his rival. The modern-day version saw Boehly and Eghbali sitting in different executive suites at games.

Chelsea fans will be hoping Boehly’s retreat might enable the club to get back on track after a messy few years. Football’s a game full of opinions and big characters. Throw in big money, and there’s plenty of opportunity for falling out.
— David Hellier
For more on the Business of Sport, check out the team’s Friday newsletter.

The two founders of Au Vodka, aged 31 and 33, are taking home at least £75 million each from the sale of the spirit brand they started shortly after leaving school, according to Bloomberg calculations. Who did they sell the company to, and how much for?
