items.title: Andy Burnham's Right Where He Didn't Want to Be: 'In Hock' to Bond Markets
body: After the early optimism of Andy Burnham’s premiership, the UK’s new prime minister now finds himself right where he didn’t want to be: at the mercy of bond markets.

Burnham’s plans for a low-key, don’t-rock-the-boat budget on Oct. 28 that would sustain the administration’s momentum in the polls is careening into higher UK borrowing costs, with economists estimating Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey will need to find £10 billion ($13.5 billion) to stabilize public finances, either by cutting spending or raising tax.

A decision from the Bank of England to slow how quickly it’s offloading its bond portfolio, effectively reducing the supply of gilts, gave yields some much-needed relief on Thursday. But the effects of the war in Iran on energy prices means borrowing costs are still substantially higher than where they were when Burnham took office two months ago.

All that means the budget is shaping up to be a harsh inflection point for Burnham and Healey, where the upbeat rhetoric that’s helped Labour register a bounce in voter opinion will have to confront Britain’s fragile economic position. While Healey’s main constituency may be the electorate, his package entails the possibility of a move to placate investors at a time when the interest paid on government borrowing is high enough to account for 10% of its spending.
“The budget is the big reckoning,” said Tom Pope, chief economist at the Institute for Government, a think tank. “The politics is hard because Burnham and Healey haven’t prepared the ground.”

Burnham appeared to take his first steps toward doing that on Wednesday, when he said the budget “is going to be challenging, because the picture around the world is challenging.” Those words marked an abrupt shift in tone for the new prime minister, who pledged on his first day in office that his administration would “bring back hope.”

It’s almost a year since Burnham broke cover in his attempts to supplant Keir Starmer. His first major intervention on that journey involved an interview where he told the New Statesman magazine, “we’ve got to get beyond this thing of being in hock to the bond markets.” The then-mayor of Manchester said he was criticizing Britain’s “low growth doom loop,” which he wanted to escape with his plan to reshape the UK economy. And yet, until that bears fruit, in office he now has to respond to those same financial forces.

What happens in markets in the next fortnight will be crucial for Healey. That’s because the Office for Budget Responsibility, which produces the economic forecasts that underpin the budget, will use a market average for key financial indicators like gilt yields from readings taken over the period.

As it stands, with the 10-year gilt yield at 5.22% on Thursday — compared to the 4.8% assumed by the OBR at the time of the last budget — Healey is estimated to have lost about half of the £23.6 billion fiscal buffer he inherited from former chancellor Rachel Reeves, according to Bloomberg Economics. That’s because higher borrowing costs mean higher debt interest payments, which constrain Healey via the government’s main fiscal rule that requires day-to-day spending to be covered by tax receipts by the end of the Parliament.

The Resolution Foundation, an influential think tank in Labour circles, estimates Healey has as little as £5 billion of fiscal headroom, when setting the increase in borrowing costs alongside other spending commitments Burnham’s announced, like his pledge to end rough sleeping and a commitment to plug a £4.7 billion hole in the government’s defense investment plan.

“Positive vibes can’t hide the painful policy trade-offs facing the chancellor,” said Sophie Hale, research director at the Resolution Foundation. Measures “to repair vital fiscal buffers” will be needed she said.

The worsening financial conditions come at a time when some critics of the government’s economic strategy are becoming more vocal. Andy Haldane, the former chief economist of the Bank of England and an unofficial adviser to Burnham as he prepared for power, told LBC Radio on Monday that markets now “suspect that this is a traditional tax-and-spend socialist government with better TikTok videos.”

Jim O’Neill, the former Goldman Sachs chief economist who also informally advised Burnham before he took office, has warned Healey against lifting taxes on businesses, saying it would risk hurting economic growth.

Those warnings come as some in the City of London were underwhelmed by their first major engagement with Healey in his new role, which offered little this week beyond the chance to stroll around Number 10 Downing Street and hear a brief speech from a chancellor preoccupied with the spike in household energy costs.
“We in government will provide the fiscal discipline and stability,” Healey told the reception of business leaders. “Together we can write the next chapter of Britain’s growth story.”

Burnham has delayed a planned investment summit that was due to take place in London to next year, with the event now set to be held outside of the UK capital, according to a person familiar with the matter. The decision to delay the summit was first reported by Sky News.

Healey’s budget preparations also suffered a setback on the news that hedge fund founder Chris Rokos, one of Britain’s top taxpayers, is set to leave the UK, putting fresh scrutiny on whether Labour is doing enough to attract and retain wealthy residents, or whether further departures are in the offing as anxiety builds over potential budget tax rises.

Sensing the government’s vulnerability on the issue, Andrew Griffith, the main opposition Conservative Party’s newly-appointed shadow chancellor, used his first major speech on Thursday to challenge the government to rule out higher taxes.

Options Healey is considering to raise revenue at the budget include higher levies on banks, oil and gas companies, and gambling firms, along with increases to the tax on capital gains, according to people familiar with the matter. Meanwhile he is looking for departmental savings to close the £4.7 billion gap in Britain’s defense investment plan.
“They’re in a very difficult position,” said Al Cattermole, fixed-income portfolio manager at Mirabaud Asset Management. “The market is very nervous.”

items.title: 'King CATL' Stranglehold on Chinese EV Makers Starts Loosening
body: Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd. has long dominated the global market for electric-vehicle batteries. Now some of its customers in China are trying to break free.

Automakers including Li Auto Inc. and Xiaomi Corp. have started to design their own cells and are adding new suppliers including Sunwoda Electronic Co. The moves have sparked concerns that a larger trend of “de-CATLization” is behind the company’s recent $100 billion market rout.

The carmakers are trying to “enhance their bargaining power” because they’re squeezed by components inflation, said Morgan Stanley analyst Tim Hsiao. “It’s a good idea and makes commercial sense to diversify.”

The push reflects the tensions between large suppliers and their customers in the world’s largest auto market, where fierce pricing competition is weighing on carmaker margins. Profits at CATL, however, have continued to grow in large part because of its outsized market dominance and pricing power.

“CATL takes all the profits, squeezing downstream automakers,” Hu Xijin, former editor-in-chief of China’s nationalist tabloid Global Times, wrote in a Weibo post this week. “There’s a saying circulating in the industry: the world has suffered under King CATL for too long.”
CATL didnt’ immediately respond to a request for comment. The company’s shares declined 0.9% in Shenzhen. They’re down 17% this year.
Read More: CATL Shares Drop 10% in Two Days as Outlook Worries Mount

Li Auto has been at the forefront of the diversification push and plans to gradually supply all of its models with self-developed batteries, it said on Sept. 7. Earlier this year, the company’s new i6 electric sedan was delayed when CATL didn’t deliver batteries on time. Li Auto had to tap alternative supplier Sunwoda to ease the bottleneck.

Xiaomi, which has long relied on batteries from CATL and BYD Co., earlier this month unveiled a new battery platform designed with two smaller producers, CALB Group Co. and Sunwoda. Called Longjia, it’s slated to go into Xiaomi’s new line of Skynomad sport utility vehicles.
With the development of autonomous driving, carmakers have also begun to focus more on developing energy systems and battery expertise in house, said Hsiao, the Morgan Stanley analyst.

“So, on one hand, it’s driven by business strategy, while on the other hand, power solutions remain very important for their future development — not only for vehicles but also for embodied AI,” he said.

items.title: Chinese Robotics Suppliers Rise on Tesla Visit Report
body: Shares of Chinese robotics‑component suppliers climbed after a local report said Tesla Inc. teams had arrived in the country to audit suppliers and place additional orders to boost production of its Optimus humanoid model.

The Solactive China Humanoid Robotics Index, which tracks companies in the sector, jumped as much as 2.4% following the report by 21st Century Business Herald. Shares of actuator maker Ningbo Tuopu Group, which rose as much as 7%, contributed the most to the index’s gain. Sensor manufacturer Ningbo Joyson Electronic Corp. and thermal-management supplier Zhejiang Sanhua Intelligent Controls Co. both advanced by more than 4%.

The stock moves highlight the key role of Chinese suppliers in robotics development worldwide. Optimism around humanoid robots has emerged as an important theme in China’s market this year, driving gains in automation and precision‑manufacturing shares.

“Tesla’s reported supplier audits are a positive commercialization signal for China’s humanoid supply chain, pointing to progress toward repeatable Optimus production,” Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Ian Ma said. “Near-term sentiment could stay supported if audits lead to confirmed supplier nominations and larger orders.”

Tesla’s teams arrived in the city of Ningbo this week for audits focused on production consistency and exclusivity requirements, the local report said, citing unnamed supply-chain sources. The US tech company, chaired by billionaire Elon Musk, has already begun placing orders from suppliers tied to the Optimus robot, the report said.
Tesla didn’t immediately respond to a Bloomberg request for comment.
While accelerating production of Optimus may lift suppliers’ near‑term outlook, Ma said earnings impact across the supply chain is likely to stay modest until robot volumes scale up.
In July, Musk said 2026 will be a ‘massive’ capex year, with plans to spend more than $25 billion and significantly expand factory operations, including the production of Optimus robots.

items.title: China Urges Stable Coal Output as Prices Rise to Three-Year High
body: China’s government urged coal miners to ensure stable production and supply after spot prices for the power-station fuel rallied to the highest level in nearly three years.

The National Development and Reform Commission, National Energy Administration, and National Mine Safety Administration recently issued a joint notice calling on coal-producing regions and companies to accelerate efforts to ensure steady output and promote the reopening of mines to support economic growth and energy supply, the NEA said in a post on its WeChat account.

Chinese coal output has fallen after a deadly accident in Shanxi province in May prompted a series of safety inspections. Coking coal for steel-making initially felt the biggest impact, with futures rising to a two-year high in early September.

Spot prices for thermal, or power-station, coal have recently surged as electricity generators stock up on supplies before a busy holiday period in the country with the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day occurring within days of each other. Prices at the hub of Qinhuangdao rose 1.9% this week to 980 yuan ($146), the highest level since October 2023.

items.title: AirAsia's Fernandes Hits Back at Critics as Stock Slumps
body: A defiant AirAsia Group Bhd. co-founder Tony Fernandes said reports Malaysia’s government has asked rivals for help were false, saying the low-cost airline will emerge from its current crisis stronger than before.

The airline’s woes have mounted this year following the outbreak of war in the Middle East, which sent oil and jet fuel prices surging. Its stock has plunged around 75% — since the conflict started amid concern the carrier is under growing financial strain. The carrier has taken the unusual step of offloading six newly-delivered planes, including two in July, Bloomberg News reported earlier.
“We’ve been through many many crises, but we’ve always come out stronger,” Fernandes said at a briefing Friday in Bangkok. “Covid was far, far worse than what we are dealing with now.”

The hastily arranged briefing came after AirAsia’s stock slumped 21% to a four-year low on Thursday after reports Malaysia’s government had asked other local airlines to potentially absorb the cash-strapped carrier’s domestic market share.

“I can say confidently the government said we never said anything like that,” Fernandes said. “You cannot just say, “Oh, this airline is going to take AirAsia’s capacity.” I mean, it’s the most ludicrous statement I have seen in 25 years.”
AirAsia had 954 million ringgit ($233 million) in cash and equivalents as of the end of June, one of the lowest balances among airlines tracked by Bloomberg globally.
“I have better things to do right now than have this press conference” because of an inaccurate article, he said. “We are good at managing cash and we are strong in liquidity,” he added.
“Things get blown out of proportion when it’s AirAsia,” Fernandes said. “I sneeze, it’s a big story.”

items.title: Strategists Say Ueda's Less-Hawkish Comments Weighed on Yen
body: The yen dropped after the Bank of Japan’s decision to hike rates as a split vote sent bearish signals, strategists said. The Japanese currency fell as much as 0.8% and bond markets erased earlier gains after the central bank raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point to 1.25%.

Board members voted 7-2 to raise the key rate in a move was predicted by all economists surveyed by Bloomberg. Investor focus now shifts to Governor Kazuo Ueda’s post-decision press conference scheduled for 3:30 p.m. Tokyo time.

items.title: Flooding Kills Three People as Heavy Rains Hit Northern Vietnam
body: Heavy rains triggered flooding and landslides across northern Vietnam, killing three people and damaging thousands of homes as well as more than 22,000 hectares of crops.

The northern region has experienced downpours since Sept. 14, with some areas receiving as much as 653 millimeters of rain, according to a statement on the government’s website. More than 16,000 of houses have been inundated while rice and other crops have been damaged.

National and provincial roads have been affected by 11 landslides and flooding in 30 locations, causing traffic tie-ups. The Hanoi-Ho Chi Minh City railway was flooded to a depth of about one meter. Several train services on the north-south railway were suspended Thursday and Friday.
In the northern coastal province of Thanh Hoa, more than 29,000 officials and soldiers were mobilized for emergency assistance.

Some Hanoi schools switched to online classes or gave students the day off Thursday as streets inundated with as much as one-meter of floodwaters caused gridlocked in the center of the capital city, state media reported. More heavy rain is expected from Thanh Hoa province to the city of Hue through the weekend, with some areas forecast to receive a deluge of over 100 millimeters.

Vietnam’s long coastline makes it vulnerable to storms roaring in from the South China Sea, while climate change and deforestation have increased the country’s potential for severe damage. As many as five more storms are expected off the coast the rest of the year, with one or two possibly sweeping over Vietnam’s mainland.

Natural disasters have killed or left 63 people missing in Vietnam in 2026, causing total losses of around 2.2 trillion dong ($84.6 million). Financial losses are down 84.9% from the same period last year when the country was hit by severe typhoons and flooding, according to separate government statement.

Meanwhile, El Nino is expected to reduce rainfall in central and southern Vietnam by 10% to 50% later this year, potentially affecting around 350,000 hectares of rice in the Mekong Delta. Severe water shortages are also forecast in the central highlands, the country’s largest coffee growing region.

items.title: Yen Extends Declines After Ueda Gives Mixed Signals on Hikes
body: The yen extended its drop against the dollar after the Bank of Japan lifted interest rates as expected, with two dissents casting doubts on the outlook for further policy tightening.

Japan’s currency fell as much as 0.7% to 157.09 per greenback, while Japanese government bonds erased earlier gains. While the move was predicted by all economists surveyed by Bloomberg, the vote was 7-2 as board members Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato dissented.
Read more: BOJ Hikes Rates at Fastest Pace Since 1990 After Bessent’s Calls

The outcome was “not hawkish enough for markets and should push USDJPY higher and front-end JPY yields lower,” said Chidu Narayanan, chief APAC strategist at Wells Fargo. “Two dissents at this meeting, albeit from the two most dovish members of the board, does not support market expectations of a slew of rapid rates hikes from the BOJ.”

Japan’s Nikkei 225 extended gains to as much as 2% in afternoon trading as the yen weakened. The Topix index was little changed as financial shares weighed on the broader gauge. Spillover in other currency and bond markets was also limited.

The BOJ’s rate increase came after the Federal Reserve’s hawkish hike earlier this week pushed the yen weaker, partly reversing a sharp rally earlier this month fueled by expectations of faster BOJ tightening, an unwind of yen-funded carry trades and speculation that Japanese pension funds could shift more money to domestic assets.
Traders will focus on BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda’s post-decision press conference, which typically starts at 3:30 p.m. in Tokyo, for clues on the pace and scope of further tightening.

“I expect a neutral-to-slightly hawkish tone, emphasizing that every meeting remains ‘live’ from here given resilient growth, persistent inflation risks and a policy rate that remains accommodative even at 1.25%,” said Masahiko Loo, senior fixed income strategist at State Street Investment Management.

Strategists say dollar-yen could climb toward 160 if investors conclude the BOJ’s tightening path will struggle to keep pace with the Fed’s. The risk is particularly acute if subsequent communication from the BOJ is interpreted as dovish, given that a quarter-point increase had already been largely priced into markets.

The latest slide also puts intervention risk back in focus after Japan and the US carried out their first coordinated yen-buying operation this summer since 1998. Officials have emphasized the speed and disorderliness of currency moves rather than any specific level, but another push toward 160 could test their tolerance.
“We should expect further Japan-US intervention in forex markets if the yen is pressured again past 160 per dollar,” said Neil Newman, head of strategy at Astris Advisory Japan.

Japan spent a record ¥15.4 trillion ($98.3 billion) on intervention in the month through Aug. 26, according to Finance Ministry data. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has since continued to signal support for a stronger yen, potentially adding to traders’ reluctance to rebuild bearish positions.

items.title: Big Iron Ore Miners Deplete Reserves Faster Than They Replace
body: The world’s biggest iron ore producers are depleting ore reserves faster than they can replenish them, as the cost and complexity of developing replacements continues to rise, according to Wood Mackenzie Ltd.

The six largest iron ore producers, which includes BHP Group and Rio Tinto Group, collectively depleted 11.1 billion tons of ore reserves that could be sold between 2016 and 2025, the consultancy said in a report released Thursday. Only three replaced the volume they mined over the period, and some spent five times more than others to add new reserves, it found.

The industry is increasingly facing an issue with grade depletion, which occurs when the average iron ore content in a mine drops as it ages and requires operators to dig deeper and invest more to extract. Miners are now reaching a point where it’s no longer about growth, but keeping operations running.

“The main challenge for the current iron ore industry is rising costs to maintain existing production,” said Mihir Vora, Wood Mackenzie’s research director for metals and mining. “The industry is investing to sustain production, but it is having to work harder to stand still.”
Read More: The World’s Biggest Iron Ore Windfall Is Fading for Australia

Costs for major miners have roughly doubled for some companies since 2016, Wood Mackenzie said. Cash margins across the industry peaked in 2021 and have since settled at around $50-$60 a ton, shrinking the margin to absorb rising costs and falling prices.

The analysis also found ore grades had fallen by as much as 1.6 percentage points among some miners since 2016. Higher-grade material is increasingly required to offset the depletion of lower-grade ore, while impurity levels, including alumina, are rising in some products.

items.title: When War Damages Cultural Treasures, What Can UNESCO Do?
body: I don’t know if artificial intelligence poses an existential threat, but the human damage to civilization’s cultural legacy is a matter of record. It continues to this day with the violent erosion of our historical heritage through war.

This week, Saudi Arabia said it intercepted a drone attack on Mecca launched from Yemen by Iran-backed Houthi rebels. The Saudis said it was the second such attempt, citing a ballistic-missile launch nine years ago. The Houthis denied firing drones toward the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad; in 2017, they said they were targeting a military installation some 40 miles from the holy city.

In April, I wrote about the risks posed to the splendid 400-year-old Shah mosque in Isfahan by US and Israeli bombing of Iran’s nearby nuclear research hub. The historic edifice hasn’t suffered a direct hit, but blast waves from the assaults have shaken tiles loose and damaged windows. The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) has designated the mosque and nearly 1,000 other cultural monuments around the world as “so exceptional as to transcend national boundaries and to be of common importance for present and future generations of all humanity.” That hasn’t prevented desecration.

Last week, two UNESCO arms released a joint report about the damage inflicted on a 1,000-year-old Hindu clifftop temple during last year’s border dispute between Thailand and Cambodia. The agency suggested those responsible could face “criminal liability” — but the legal, evidentiary and regulatory hurdles to pursuing that route are laborious. Despite surviving centuries of depredation, these priceless relics rarely have the luxury of time.

At least two international courts have adjudicated on the Thai-Cambodia quarrel, recognizing the promontory hosting the ancient Preah Vihear temple as Cambodian. But they left open the question of who owns the surrounding territory, which sits directly on the frontier between the two nations. And so the fighting engulfed the entire area, including the temple. A photo published by UNESCO appears to show the collapse of the front of one ornamental gateway in the complex.

Criminal liability was also a potential recourse in 2024 after Israeli bombing in Lebanon came close to the 2,000-year-old Temple of Jupiter in Baalbek and the archaeological zones of Tyre, which include Roman baths and crusader fortifications. Instead, Lebanese officials requested — and eventually received — what’s called “enhanced protection” from UNESCO’s Committee for the Protection of Cultural Property in the Event of Armed Conflict. That adds an additional level of moral opprobrium to any attack that vandalizes the sites. Lebanon pledged that the locations wouldn’t be used for military purposes.

But ethical qualms aren’t enough to deter destruction, especially when non-state actors are involved. From 2015 to 2017, the terrorist group Islamic State demolished several temples in the ancient Syrian city of Palmyra. These included the Temple of BelThe name of the Palmyrene god Bel derives from the semitic word Baal (Lord) that was a generic name for the pagan rivals of the monotheistic deity of ancient Israel., which was dedicated in the year 32, arguably within the lifetime of Jesus of Nazareth. It predated the Colosseum in Rome. The battles that eventually retook the site from ISIS further despoiled Palmyra.

Criminal prosecutions may be easier if the antagonists are not nation states — and you can identify specific assailants. In 2012, Islamist fighters associated with Al-Qaeda smashed most of the historic mausoleums in the city of Timbuktu in Mali, some of which date to the 13th century. The episode produced the only conviction of any person for the war crime of heritage destruction: Ahmad Al Faqi Al Mahdi, the head of the Ansar Dine militia’s morality police during its 10-month occupation of the city. He was imprisoned first in the Netherlands and then in Scotland; his whereabouts since completing his sentence (nine years reduced to seven) are unknown.

Although a legal precedent was established, no comparable punishments have followed. In the meantime, the tombs — traditionally constructed of mud in the manner of the Great Mosque of Djenne to the south of Timbuktu — have been rebuilt.

Even if it falls short of providing protection in times of war, UNESCO’s list of heritage sites embodies our reverence for the past, appealing to primal instincts that are the opposite of carnage: preservation and remembrance.

Take the Dormition Cathedral in Kyiv. Built in the 11th century, it went through several alterations before suffering a catastrophic fire in the 18th century. Rebuilt shortly afterwards with baroque splendor, it was destroyed again in 1941 either by occupying Nazis or opposing resistance forces. It remained a ruin for six decades until Ukraine became independent following the collapse of the Soviet Union. The cathedral’s UNESCO-approved reconstruction was completed in 2000.
And then, on June 15, 2026, a Russian drone attack set the cathedral roof on fire and damaged the interior.

AI is trained on human knowledge and thus absorbs human foibles — but surely something of our nobler selves can also be incorporated. I can only hope that UNESCO’S records feed into the models and can influence computer-directed military operations to avoid attacking these communal treasures.

items.title: The $2.4 Billion Legacy Project Changing Belgrade
body: Every few weeks, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic visits the sprawling EXPO 2027 construction site just outside Belgrade to check on the $2.4 billion investment seen locally as his legacy project, and to update his social media followers on the progress.

As he stood by massive steel plinths in late July, trucks transported sand to and from the future pavilions of more than 140 countries. The event — the biggest of its kind in the Western Balkans since the wars that tore up former Yugoslavia three decades ago — will serve as an “engine that will drive development” from tourism and hospitality to construction, transport and trade, Vucic said in an Instagram video.

He has also said he hopes that it will help recast Serbia’s image. Action movie star Jackie Chan, Olympic gold medalist Usain Bolt, Chinese badminton champion Lin Dan, as well as Serbia’s own Jelena Jankovic, a former top-ranked tennis player, serve as brand ambassadors.

When the three-month-long exhibition – ‘Play for Humanity: Sport and Music for All’ – ends in August, the complex is slated to become a new suburb of the capital, with thousands of apartments, a rail link to the airport, and a dock on the Sava River. A sports stadium big enough to seat 52,000 people will be completed in 2028, ready to host the UEFA Europa League final a year later.

Vucic wants to see the project through to completion, but he and his ruling Progressive Party would need to win an election next month. He has called a snap parliamentary vote for Oct. 25 as he plans to step down as president and run for prime minister in a bid to extend his hold on power over the nation of 6.6 million people. Some polls indicate it’s a tight race that he may lose.

Vucic has dominated Serbia’s politics for more than a decade. During that time the country attracted more foreign investment than any other in the western Balkans as he balanced ties between the European Union, Russia, China and the US. The economy doubled to around $99.95 billion. But he’s facing mounting public discontent with his rule.

Over the past two years, student-led protests have grown into a mass movement that has now entered electoral politics. Its candidates promise to battle corruption, improve the rule of law and judicial independence, expand labor rights and ensure better access to health care and education.

Such tensions have made EXPO 2027 a lightning rod for political opponents, who see the event as a way for the ruling administration to siphon off public funds, while increasing public debt and widening the wealth gap between Belgrade and the provinces.

Five small opposition groups, including the People’s Movement of Serbia, have called on the Paris-based Bureau International des Expositions, which chose Belgrade, to cancel the exhibition. They also warned about “risks to the security and health” of participants, citing the concrete canopy collapse at a renovated train station in 2024 that killed 16 people.

Those worries surfaced in a European Parliament report on Serbia last year, which urged participants to “take into account the serious concerns and evidence of widespread corruption linked to the ruling authorities, as well as the reported lack of compliance with basic construction standards and legal requirements in the organization and construction.”
The authorities have dismissed the claims as politically motivated and baseless.

The 25 hectare- (62 acre-) exhibition site used to be farmland. Serbia is investing €1.23 billion ($1.4 billion) in its transformation into fairgrounds, and another €700 million in related infrastructure, according to EXPO 2027, the state company overseeing the preparations. Fees for the brand ambassadors haven’t been disclosed, and the organizers say the celebrities will be paid by unspecified sponsors.

Around 1.6 million visitors are expected at the event. The Belgrade-based Louis Berger Adria consultancy estimated it will generate more than €9 billion in new value for the economy by 2037 and €3.8 billion in tax revenues over 10 years. It said that every dinar of public investment may generate 1.91 dinars in tax revenue, along with boosting employment.
“It’s been an enormous challenge but the benefits are even bigger,” said EXPO 2027 director Danilo Jerinic in an interview.

Serbia has selected PowerChina as the main contractor, and has asked the Beijing-based company to add a thousand more laborers to ensure pavilions are ready by December, according to Jerinic. More than 4,000 people are already working in three shifts around the clock, he said.

After the exhibition, around 700 hectares of adjacent land will be offered to private companies, mainly real estate developers. Residents of this new area will have access to schools, retail and office space, as well as the Nikola Tesla airport rail link. And, by reinforcing the Sava River embankment with a port, a waterborne route to central Belgrade.

Such a carefully planned urban space would mark a break from practices of the past three decades, when authorities often turned a blind eye to structures built without permits or planning, leading to shanty town-style suburbs near cities, including the capital.
For Jerinic, “the EXPO will be an example of how to activate a completely new location in a city.”

items.title: Copper Set for Weekly Gain as Chinese Buyers Return to the Fore
body: Copper headed for a weekly gain, as signs of a rebound in Chinese demand helped to offset hawkish messaging from the Federal Reserve about the likelihood of more interest rate rises.

Benchmark futures were little changed near $14,460 a ton on the London Metal Exchange on Friday, on pace for the 11th weekly advance in the past 12. That streak saw the metal advance to a record earlier this month.

In China, the Yangshan premium — a gauge of demand named after the port in Shanghai that’s a major entry point for imported copper — rose to $121 a ton on Thursday, the highest level since November 2022. Meanwhile, domestic copper production fell slightly in August from the month before.

Copper has risen 16% this year as bets that the Trump administration would hit refined metal with tariffs triggered a surge of imports into the US, squeezing availability elsewhere. This week’s hike by the Fed — the first since 2023 — had little impact, even with hawkish messaging on the scope for further tightening. Higher rates typically damp demand for non-yielding assets like commodities.

“We expect base metals to remain mostly range-bound in the coming weeks, as supply-side risks offset a fragile macro backdrop,” analysts at BMI, a Fitch Solutions company, said in a note. “Markets continue to wait for a firm decision on US copper tariffs.”
Copper was 0.2% lower at $14,458.50 a ton on the LME at 10:57 a.m. in Singapore. Other metals were little changed, with aluminum declining 0.3%.
Iron ore added 0.8% to $97.15 a ton in Singapore, rising for a third day.

items.title: BOJ Rate Hike Fails to Buoy Yen Even As Ueda Signals More Moves
body: The Bank of Japan raised its benchmark interest rate, ramping up the pace of hikes to the fastest in 36 years as it confronts mounting inflation risks and unusually explicit calls for further policy normalization from Washington.

The BOJ lifted its policy rate by a quarter point to 1.25% Friday at the end of a two-day meeting, according to its statement, in a move predicted by all economists surveyed by Bloomberg. The vote was 7-2 as board members Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato dissented.
The yen weakened to 156.95 against the dollar after the highly telegraphed move, with no strong sign of more hawkish language in the statement to fuel bullish bets on Japan’s currency.

The move, coming just three months after the BOJ’s previous increase, marks the shortest interval between rate hikes since 1990, when the central bank’s rapid policy tightening played a key role in bursting Japan’s asset bubble. It was the sixth rate increase under Governor Kazuo Ueda — the most by any BOJ chief in at least half a century — and came after a wave of US pressure from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to push up rates.

The BOJ’s accelerated pace of hikes comes after a shift in the global backdrop for monetary policy as authorities address the fallout from the Iran war. The Federal Reserve underscored the change Wednesday with its first rate hike in three years, while also penciling in another move later this year, and the European Central Bank raised rates last week for the second time this year.

The latest hike in Japan marks the first time that the BOJ, Fed and ECB have all raised borrowing costs in the same month. The synchronized moves also underscore how far the BOJ has come from its longtime status as a global monetary policy outlier.
The increase came as little surprise after a salvo of remarks from Bessent helped cement market expectations for a move.

While the yen weakened against the dollar shortly after the announcement, it remains stronger than its levels in July after coordinated intervention by the US and Japan at the end of that month helped push it further from the roughly 40-year low of 163.99 set on July 23.

The BOJ reiterated its stance that it would continue raising rates if its outlook for the economy and prices is realized. At 1.25%, the policy rate would for the first time sit inside the lower end of the bank’s estimated range for the neutral rate, a level considered neither stimulative nor restrictive.

Bessent’s repeated remarks supporting BOJ action in the run-up to the board meeting helped fuel expectations for a rate increase, with the move almost fully priced in by early September. In a face-to-face meeting with Ueda in North Carolina last month, Bessent “expressed strong support” for Japan’s decisive steps to address the weakening of the yen, according to the Treasury Department.

Japan’s key inflation gauge remained above 2% for a fourth straight year through 2025, and the BOJ expects inflation to stay above its target in coming years. Data released earlier Friday showed that core inflation slowed a tad in August thanks partly to distortions from subsidies. Analysts expect price gains to accelerate toward 3% by early next year.
Ueda is set to explain the thinking behind Friday’s decision and the trajectory for rates in the months ahead at a press briefing that usually begins at 3:30 p.m.

items.title: Tata Sons Power Struggle Deepens as Chandra's Return a Setback for Noel
body: Good morning... I’m Pratigya Vajpayee in New Delhi, wrapping up the week in markets for you.Tata Group shares stole the show in an otherwise lackluster session on Thursday. They are likely to stay in the spotlight today as well after Tata Sons’ board said it would pursue a stock listing and give its chairman another five-year term despite strong opposition from the founding-family patriarch (more on that below).Meanwhile, India’s benchmark NSE Nifty 50 Index continues to struggle. The gauge is on course to extend a five-week losing streak as foreign funds remain net sellers. In the bond market, yields rose after the central bank sold 500 billion rupees of bonds to drain excess cash from the financial system.Investors will be hoping positive regional cues lend support. Asian stocks and bonds have edged higher early on Friday as a pullback in oil prices eased inflation concerns. The region’s biggest event today is the Bank of Japan’s policy decision. The central bank is set to raise its benchmark interest rate, delivering its most closely spaced rate increases since 1990.In today’s newsletter, we write about:

The Tata Sons board on Thursday approved going public by a majority vote and asked Chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran to stay on for five more years. But the listing and succession saga at India’s oldest conglomerate may have more twists and turns in store.The board’s decisions are a sharp setback for patriarch Noel Tata, who has long fought to keep the holding company private. While Chandrasekaran, widely known as Chandra, agreed to stay on, Tata Trusts — the controlling shareholder of Tata Sons led by Noel — called the board’s decision on his reappointment “illegal.” In a separate statement late on Thursday, the Trusts — a group of 13 charities — said they had not agreed to a listing and that the company’s board had to explore all available options.That sets the stage for a showdown. A public float would bring far greater regulatory and market scrutiny to Tata Sons. For Tata Trusts, the move risks diluting its ability to fend off any hostile takeover attempts. For minority shareholder Shapoorji Pallonji Group, however, it provides a path to monetize its holding and reduce costly debt.At the same board meeting, Noel had presented a proposal from the SP Group to monetize part of its stake in Tata Sons in a deal that would raise at least 250 billion rupees ($2.6 billion), according to the Tata Trusts’ statement. The proposal envisages a share buyout in two tranches over 18 months, with Noel suggesting the funds could come from internal cash flows, sales of listed shares or stakes in newer businesses.Despite the power struggle, group stocks reacted positively to the developments on Thursday. Tata Chemicals jumped more than 13% to a four-month high. Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles climbed as much as 6.3%, while Tata Consultancy Services rose 3.4%. Tata Investment Corp. surged 7.6%.
IPO market heats up with NSE in focus

India’s primary market showed renewed vigor as investors bid for the National Stock Exchange’s IPO, with the $2.4 billion offering being subscribed 42% on the first day. Meanwhile, six relatively small companies made their trading debuts, with most posting solid first-day gains. Karamtara Engineering surged as much as 39% above its offer price, while Rentomojo jumped as much as 29%, putting the online rental platform on track for one of the strongest debuts this year among Indian IPOs that raised at least $100 million. Steamhouse India also climbed as much as 29%, while LCC Projects rallied about 15%. Asset Reconstruction Co. India and Manipal Payment and Identity Solutions bucked the trend, closing slightly below their IPO prices.
Staples firms grapple with pricey inputs: Yes Securities

Expensive raw materials are threatening a recovery in consumer staples firms’ margins this year, according to Yes Securities. Crude oil, cocoa, sugar, palm oil and dairy are driving costs higher, while international freight remains expensive. The impact, however, will be company specific, the brokerage says. Britannia has some protection from its procurement strategy, while Varun Beverages benefits from its portfolio mix. Nestlé and Colgate are leaning more on productivity gains and cost savings, while HUL and Dabur are using price increases to rebuild margins.
UPI fee to boost valuations for Paytm, Pine Labs: Emkay

NPCI’s move to start charging merchants for larger UPI payments could give payment firms a more predictable source of revenue, Emkay says. Using conservative assumptions about how much of the merchant discount rate Paytm and Pine Labs ultimately retain, the brokerage estimates the new charge could generate 11.2 billion rupees of UPI revenue for Paytm and 1.55 billion rupees for Pine Labs in fiscal 2028. The additional earnings stream materially raises its valuations for both companies, Emkay says, lifting its price targets for Paytm’s stock to 2,400 rupees and for Pine Labs to 230 rupees while retaining buy ratings on both.

The Federal Reserve’s hawkish rate hike has reinforced expectations that the RBI may not be able to stay on hold much longer. Elevated Treasury yields make global investors demand higher returns from emerging markets such as India, while a narrowing rate differential risks adding pressure on the rupee. That gives the RBI less room to tolerate rising inflation or let the gap with US yields shrink further. India’s swap market is already pricing in more than 75 basis points of increases in overnight rates by December, as traders expect the central bank to drain excess liquidity and raise policy rates with oil holding above $100 a barrel.

items.title: Malaysia Airlines Closing in on Order for Boeing 787 Dreamliners
body: Malaysia Airlines’s parent is said to be closing in on an order for Boeing Co. 787 Dreamliners as the carrier seeks to renew its long-haul fleet, according to people familiar with the matter.

Malaysia Aviation Group is likely to place an order for about ten 787-10s, the people said, asking not to be identified because the discussions are confidential. Boeing edged out Airbus SE by offering earlier delivery slots starting in 2031, with GE Aviation offering better terms on the engines compared with Rolls-Royce Holdings Plc, some of the people said.

The new 787s will replace the airline’s seven leased Airbus A350 jets while also providing room for future growth, the people said. Malaysia Airlines has been looking to replace the A350s due to high lease rentals, and the airline evaluated planes from both manufacturers for the order, the people said.

The deal also has political undertones because US President Donald Trump has tied Boeing orders to trade pacts he signed with various countries. Trump and Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced last year that the country would purchase 30 Boeing aircraft with options for 30 more.
Malaysia Aviation Group did not immediately respond to requests for a response. Boeing and Airbus declined to comment.

Malaysia Airlines has relied on Airbus for its widebody planes since 2016, using older A330s and newer A350s when it retired the Boeing 777 from service. The company ordered forty A330neos in recent years to replace its oldest jets, with 10 already now delivered among its roughly 90-strong fleet which includes fifty-seven 737 single-aisle jets.

items.title: Waymo Plans to Offer Paid Robotaxi Rides in Singapore in 2028
body: Waymo plans to offer its robotaxi service in Singapore in 2028, the latest in a string of domestic and international expansions by the Alphabet Inc. unit.

The Mountain View, California-based company will bring a fleet of Jaguar I-PACE electric vehicles to the Asian city-state in the coming months, it said in a statement late Thursday in the US.  Starting next year, its trained specialists will manually drive the vehicles to map and learn Singapore’s roads and monsoon weather patterns, it added.

Waymo offers paid service in 15 US cities and has been preparing to launch internationally, including in London, Tokyo and Germany. The company has also registered operations in France, the Netherlands and Spain, though it has yet to announce commercial plans. It has begun paid rides in several markets recently, including Las Vegas this week and Denver, San Diego, and Tampa, Florida, earlier this month.

When it opens service to the Singaporean public in 2028, Waymo plans to make its vehicles available on its own consumer app. That’s a different approach from Chinese rivals like WeRide Inc. and Pony AI Inc., which have launched small-scale services in the city-state by partnering with local ride-hailing apps, such as Grab Holdings Ltd. and ComfortDelGro Corp Ltd.

It is unclear whether Waymo will operate limited routes in Singapore similar to ones offered by other robotaxi providers. Waymo said in the statement that its service will complement that market’s public transit network by bridging “first-and-last-mile transit gaps across residential and commercial hubs.”

The company plans to manually map all the regions of Singapore and collect the necessary data to seek Land Transport Authority approval for its autonomous driving system in 2027, a Waymo spokesperson said.

items.title: Yuan Hits Four-Year High as PBOC Signals Support Before Trump-Xi
body: The yuan climbed to its strongest level in more than four years as China’s central bank continued to guide the currency higher ahead of a meeting between Chinese leader Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump.

The offshore yuan gained as much as 0.1% to 6.6957 per dollar on Friday, the strongest since July 2022. The move came after the People’s Bank of China strengthened its daily currency fixing for an eighth straight session, the longest streak since 2023.

The timing puts the yuan in focus ahead of the Trump-Xi meeting next week, with trade tensions likely to feature prominently. A stronger currency could help ease some friction, with Western officials arguing that an undervalued yuan gives Chinese exports a competitive advantage and contributes to the country’s record trade surplus.

“The renminbi is likely to receive further support from the Trump-Xi summit,” said Serena Zhou, senior economist at Mizuho Securities Asia Ltd. She expects the offshore yuan to end September around 6.70 per dollar and maintained her year-end forecast of 6.65.

Zhou said expectations for yuan appreciation have become “increasingly self-reinforcing” despite slowing Chinese growth and rising bets on Federal Reserve rate hikes, while Beijing appears more tolerant of a gradual strengthening as it seeks to promote the currency’s internationalization.
Still, the PBOC has kept its daily reference rates weaker than prevailing market levels, suggesting officials favor a measured appreciation rather than a rapid move higher.

That approach is consistent with the central bank’s emphasis on currency stability. Deputy Governor Lu Lei said this month that the PBOC will firmly maintain yuan stability through 2030, while emphasizing that China has neither the need nor the intention to seek a trade advantage through depreciation as exports have become less sensitive to exchange-rate moves.

The yuan is now heading for a seventh straight quarterly gain, making it Asia’s best-performing currency this year. China’s surging exports and robust conversion flows have supported the rally, which has persisted even as rising bets on Fed rate hikes have pushed Treasury yields and the dollar higher, widening the China-US yield gap to a record.

“We expect CNH to outperform in Asia given its relatively low dependence on imported energy and strategic energy inventory,” said Abbas Keshvani, Asia macro strategist at RBC Capital Markets. “It also helps that the PBOC tends to marshal the currency stable through periods of volatility.”

items.title: Strapped AirAsia Takes Unusual Step of Offloading New Planes
body: AirAsia Group Bhd. has sold six newly-delivered aircraft since the start of last year, including two in July, in an unusual about-face that points to the financial strain gripping the airline.

The Malaysian low-cost carrier, which has received 10 factory-fresh Airbus SE 321neos since the start of 2025, sold half a dozen of them to lessor BBAM LLC, according to a Bloomberg News analysis of aircraft transactions tracked by the Cirium Fleet Analyzer database. They have since been purchased or leased by Vietnamese startup Sun PhuQuoc Airways, the data shows.

While airlines regularly execute sale-and-leaseback deals on new planes to replace large upfront purchase costs with regular lease payments, selling aircraft without ever having put them into service is uncommon. AirAsia’s disposal of the new-generation fuel-efficient jets come at a time that co-founder Tony Fernandes is seeking to modernize the fleet to combat higher fuel costs.

“It’s unusual for a newly delivered aircraft in AirAsia’s livery to not enter service with only the ‘sale’ and no ‘leaseback,’” independent aviation capital markets analyst Andrew Light said. “Selling a newly delivered aircraft is probably the cleanest option, especially to maximize cash.”
AirAsia and its management team didn’t respond to repeated requests for comment. BBAM, Sun PhuQuoc Airways and its parent Sun Group, also didn’t respond to requests for a response.
Read More: AirAsia Plunges To Four-Year Low on Route Absorption Report

The airline’s woes have mounted this year following the outbreak of war in the Middle East, which sent oil and jet fuel prices surging. Low-cost carriers can be harder hit than full-service airlines by rising fuel costs because they are harder to pass on to price-conscious passengers. AirAsia doesn’t hedge its fuel purchases, leaving it exposed to volatile swings in prices.

Fuel expenses surged 58% in the second quarter, sparking the company’s largest quarterly loss in four years. Bloomberg reported this week that AirAsia is seeking to use collateral on a private-credit loan to pay lessors. In June, Bloomberg reported that the airline had fallen behind on payments to suppliers and asked for deferrals on at least a dozen planes.
AirAsia had 954 million ringgit ($233 million) in cash and equivalents as of the end of June, one of the lowest balances among airlines tracked by Bloomberg globally.

The shares have slumped more than 75% since the Iran war started at the end of February, making it the worst-performing stock in the 58-member Bloomberg World Airlines Index. They fell as much 6.9% on Friday, after tumbling 21% on Thursday amid mounting concerns about the company’s prospects.
Meanwhile, Tony Fernandes, co-founder of AirAsia, said at a briefing on Friday that recent media coverage of the company was causing a “ripple effect” and said that its liquidity was strong.
AirAsia Says Liquidity Is Strong, Third-Quarter Bookings Hit 80%

Of the 239 Airbus planes in AirAsia’s fleet at the end of June, only 161 were operational, according to the company. The airline said it was returning 25 older aircraft this year to optimize its fleet, however, it has made no mention of the disposal of brand new planes.

Cirium’s database shows Vietnam’s Sun PhuQuoc Airways has expanded to a fleet of 19 aircraft since its launch in November 2025. A total of 14 planes it has bought or leased have come directly from AirAsia. Cirium records don’t include AirAsia’s most recent July delivery, which is still in AirAsia’s possession but will be transferred to Sun PhuQuoc in October.

items.title: Indian Project Financier's Data Center Loans Top $1.2 Billion
body: India’s top state-run infrastructure financier has sanctioned loans upwards of 30 billion rupees ($313 million) each to at least four data centers, reflecting the nation’s push to participate in the artificial intelligence buildout.

The facilities from the National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development, or Nabfid, have a moratorium of as much as five years, with repayment over the following 10 years, Managing Director Rajkiran Rai G. said in an interview.
Such projects generate “good” cash flows despite long construction periods, he said, adding that Nabfid has seen good traction from hyperscalers or large cloud services providers.

Demand for such loans signals growing corporate spending on large projects such as data centers in India. Global investors from EQT AB and Blackstone Inc. to Alphabet Inc., alongside local conglomerates like Adani Group, have also committed billions of dollars to set up AI compute infrastructure in the country.
Nabfid estimates that India’s data centers will need about 1 trillion rupees in funding through March 2031, according to its presentation.
The lender, which is looking to diversify borrowing sources, has readied its maiden dollar bond after the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates this week.
The lender plans to raise 1 trillion rupees in the year through March, with about 40% coming from overseas by end-December, Rai said.

Nabfid raised close to $1 billion in offshore loans under the central bank’s concessional window available till Dec. 31, and has mandated foreign banks to mobilize a 10-year dollar bond of a similar amount through the window by the end of this month, Rai said.

items.title: Thailand Power Demand Growth Set for Nine-Year High on AI Boom
body: Thailand expects electricity demand to grow at the fastest pace since at least 2018, fueled by industrial activity including electronics production amid a global boom in artificial intelligence and data-center investment.

Electricity consumption is forecast to increase 5.3% in 2026, the highest growth rate in nine years, according to the Energy Policy and Planning Office. Overall energy use is also expected to rise, supported by electronics exports, public investment and domestic consumption.

The surge highlights a growing challenge for Thailand as it attracts technology investment that is both boosting manufacturing and placing greater demands on the country’s power system. Electronics producers are expanding output of components used in global technology and data-center supply chains, while billions of dollars of new data-center projects are creating an additional source of future electricity demand.
Read More: AI Boom Set to Lift Thai Exports to Record Value This Year

Domestic energy consumption rose 6% in the first half, led by industry, which accounted for more than 40% of total use. Electronics manufacturing was among the biggest contributors to the increase, followed by auto production, according to the Energy Ministry data. Energy use also increased among businesses including retailers, hotels and other tourism-related operators.

Thailand has emerged as a beneficiary of the global AI investment boom as demand rises for electronics used in computing and data-center infrastructure. The International Monetary Fund has identified the country among Asian economies benefiting from the technology cycle through its electronics exports.

The growing power requirements come as Thailand is reassessing how quickly it can accommodate the technology investment. The government recently halted dozens of data-center projects while it develops new regulations covering their electricity and water use.
Read More: Thailand Puts 49 Data Centers on Hold Over Resource Strain

items.title: Jailed Ex-Malaysian PM Najib's Bid for Royal Pardon Said to Be Reviewed Friday
body: Malaysia’s jailed former premier Najib Razak’s bid for another royal intervention in his corruption conviction linked to the multibillion dollar 1MDB scandal will be considered Friday by the country’s Pardons Board, which is headed by the Malaysian king, according to people familiar with the matter.
The Pardons Board will discuss Najib’s pardon application just a week after deferring the matter, the people said, asking not to be identified because the information is private.

Singapore’s Straits Times earlier reported on the Pardons Board meeting. The newspaper said the decision to reconvene the board so soon was highly unusual, with Najib’s application expected to be the only item on the agenda.

The Pardons Board deferred a decision on Najib’s application at its Sept. 11 meeting, saying it would be considered at a future sitting. The meeting coincided with the annual general assembly of the United Malays National Organisation, a party that Najib once led and has called for his release. Party President Ahmad Zahid Hamidi expressed disappointment over the delay while appealing for a favorable outcome for the former premier, given his enduring popularity among party members.

Any fresh royal intervention risks widening divisions between UMNO and Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s Pakatan Harapan alliance, whose rise to power was fueled in part by public anger over the 1MDB scandal. Pakatan Harapan said in a statement last week that those convicted of corruption or abuse of power, particularly in high-profile cases, should serve the full sentences imposed by the courts, without naming Najib specifically.

Najib’s lawyer and an aide didn’t respond to requests for comment. Hannah Yeoh, a cabinet minister who sits on the Pardons Board, also didn’t respond to a request for comment. A representative for the national palace didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Najib was ousted in 2018 elections as the fallout from 1MDB ended UMNO’s six-decade hold on power. The former premier, who has been in prison since August 2022, may return to politics if he’s pardoned and allowed out of jail, his lawyer said last year.

In early 2024, then-King Sultan Abdullah Ahmad Shah halved Najib’s 12-year prison sentence and reduced his fines shortly before his reign ended under Malaysia’s rotational monarchy. Najib said that Sultan Abdullah, who hails from his home state of Pahang, had also issued a supplementary royal order allowing him to serve the rest of his sentence under house arrest.
In December, a court rejected Najib’s bid to serve the rest of his jail term at home. He challenged the decision, but withdrew the appeal in April without giving a reason.

A Malaysian court sentenced him to a further 15 years in prison after finding him guilty on all 25 charges of abuse of power and money laundering linked to the failed state investment fund, formally known as 1Malaysia Development Bhd. The court also imposed an 11.4 billion ringgit ($2.8 billion) fine. He has appealed both the conviction and sentence.

items.title: Indonesian Tycoon Close to Prabowo Creates Coal Mining Giant
body: Indonesian tycoon Andi Syamsuddin Arsyad agreed to acquire a major stake in miner PT Bayan Resources, setting the stage for him to become one of the biggest players in the global coal industry.

The billionaire, better known as Haji Isam, has been seeking control of Bayan in a deal that would make him one of the world’s top coal producers. He was among the biggest backers of Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto’s 2024 election campaign and now oversees major government projects, including a 1-million-hectare food estate in Papua.

Haji Isam agreed on Sept. 16 to acquire 30% of Bayan’s shares through his company PT Jhonlin Baratama, according to a stock exchange filing late Thursday. The shares will be transferred from Low Tuck Kwong and his daughter Elaine Low, Bayan’s two biggest shareholders, subject to several conditions.

Bayan didn’t elaborate further on the deal or the price of the share sale in the filing. The company’s stock rose as much as 20% in Jakarta on Friday, the biggest intraday gain in a month, and was set for a weekly advance of around 12%.

Jhonlin and Bayan didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. Haji Isam made a $3 billion cash offer for a 62% stake in the coal company earlier this month, according to people familiar with the matter. That offer put a price tag of roughly $4.8 billion on Bayan.

Haji Isam’s conglomerate PT Jhonlin Group is already a major producer of thermal coal, requesting a mining quota of 60 million tons this year, Bloomberg reported in July. Bayan, meanwhile, mined about 68 million tons last year.
Read More: Prabowo’s Favored Tycoon Wants to Become Indonesia’s Richest Man

The combined total would place Haji Isam above industry giants like Glencore Plc and below only Indian and Chinese miners that sell their product domestically. If he gets a controlling stake in Bayan, the 49-year-old from Kalimantan would oversee by far the largest coal business in Indonesia, the world’s biggest exporter of the fossil fuel.

Market participants are now waiting for more details of the transaction to gauge the impact on the company’s share price, said Andreas Yordan Tarigan, an equity analyst at PT Sucor Sekuritas. “But the market has been waiting excitedly for this to happen. It’s always exciting when there’s a jumbo transaction happening,” he said.

Bayan, founded by Singapore-born Low in 2004, had its production quota slashed by the Indonesian government earlier this year, leading it to declare force majeure last week. Competitors including PT Bumi Resources and PT Adaro Andalan were largely spared from enforced output cuts, Bloomberg reported in February.

Haji Isam has quickly become one of Prabowo’s favorite businessmen, with the Indonesian president flying to the entrepreneur’s coastal hometown of Batulicin the day after he was sworn in to express his gratitude. Considering most of Haji Isam’s businesses are unlisted, his fortune is hard to pin down, but people who know him say it easily exceeds $1 billion.

items.title: Traders Eye Xi-Trump Meet for Clues on AI Rivalry, Yuan Outlook
body: Artificial intelligence, a lingering trade war and the yuan will likely dominate the agenda of the upcoming US-China summit, with focus on whether the two nations can reach concessions or put guardrails around key areas of competition, analysts say.
For now, markets are sending mixed signals about the outcome of next week’s meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping.

Indicating cautious optimism, a Goldman Sachs Group Inc. survey shows 46% of offshore and 38% of onshore investors expect Chinese stocks to rise after the talks. Only a small minority foresees losses. Meanwhile, overseas exchange-traded fund flows and options positioning suggest foreign investors remain wary ahead of the summit, according to Tony Lee, JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s equity-derivatives strategist.

AI is widely expected to be a central topic as the technology race turns increasingly heated, with access to advanced US chips, safety standards and disputes over the pace of the industry’s development among key points of contention. The fate of a soon-to-expire one-year tariff truce, Beijing’s export curbs on rare earths, as well as the value of China’s currency may also be in the spotlight.
Here’s a closer look at what investors are watching ahead of the event:

The two countries’ tech rivalry has become more intense lately, with Beijing criticizing calls among leading US industry executives to slow AI development and impose tighter curbs on Chinese model makers as fearmongering and confrontation.
It risks weighing further on Chinese AI firms from Z.AI Co. and MiniMax Group Inc., whose stocks have been under pressure in recent months due to fierce competition and concerns over cash burn.

“Ultimately, both leaders know that AI is critical for national security, so neither is likely to slow its efforts and each will seek to undermine the other,” said Vey-Sern Ling,  a managing director at Union Bancaire Privée. “Any loosening of semiconductor restrictions will be positive for both countries, especially for Nvidia, and China’s large language model developers such as Alibaba, Tencent and Zhipu.”

Expectations are high that the summit may result in an extension of the bilateral trade truce that will expire in November, after the two nations have started talks over slashing tariffs on certain goods, including on American energy and agricultural shipments, as well as lower duties on Chinese inputs for manufacturers.

With representatives from state-owned food trading firm Cofco likely to join President Xi’s delegation, investors will be watching for fresh Chinese orders for US agricultural products such as soybean, analysts say. The potential for BYD Co. to feature in the trade mission also has drawn interest in Chinese electric-vehicle makers’ access to the US market.

A major sticking point in the bilateral relations, access to Chinese rare earths will likely remain high on the agenda. Any easing by Beijing on export restrictions could help downstream manufacturers, while reducing some of the scarcity premium in alternative suppliers, Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Markets, wrote in a note.
The yuan may also be discussed at the summit, especially after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in August that many people considered the Chinese currency undervalued.

The yuan has strengthened around 4% against the dollar this year, making itself Asia’s top performer. Despite the gains, Beijing also faces criticism from European countries such as Germany for using an artificially cheap currency to gain an unfair trade advantage.

While some analysts expect China to allow the yuan to see modest gains in the coming days to help create a more conducive environment for the summit, it’s unlikely to tolerate significant appreciation given the country’s reliance on a robust export machine to keep its economy humming.

“China’s strategy has been maintaining currency stability at a reasonable level, and this does not look likely to change even if there is external pressure,” said Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING Bank NV.

items.title: Immunology Drugmaker Electra Raises $350 Million in Upsized IPO
body: Electra Therapeutics Inc., a clinical-stage developer of immunology drugs, raised $350 million in an upsized US initial public offering priced at the mid-point of its marketed range.

The OrbiMed-backed firm sold 23.3 million shares for $15 each, according to a statement Thursday. Electra had offered 21.67 million shares for $14 to $16 apiece, its filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission show.

The offering was multiple times oversubscribed, Bloomberg News reported. At the IPO price, the San Francisco-based company would have a market value of roughly $941.5 million, based on the outstanding shares in the filings.

Electra’s lead drug candidate is designed to treat secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, a severe immune system overreaction. The company is conducting a global mid-stage trial of the drug in newly diagnosed patients, according to its filing. The therapy has received a Breakthrough Therapy designation from the US Food and Drug Administration as well as a Priority Medicine designation from the European Medicines Agency.

The IPO will hit the US market at an exuberant time for drug developers. Listings of biotech and pharmaceutical companies have raised $6.8 billion this year, versus $1.3 billion in the corresponding period in 2025, data compiled by Bloomberg show.

The company’s investors include entities affiliated with OrbiMed, Westlake BioPartners and Redmile Group. Electra raised about $182.7 million from a Series C funding round in October, led by a unit of French drugmaker Sanofi SA, OrbiMed and Redmile and carried $97.7 million of cash and equivalents at of June 30 this year, according to the filings.
The firm had a net loss of $58.6 million for the six months ended June 30, compared to a net loss of $25.4 million for the same period a year prior, the filings show.

Electra’s offering was led by Jefferies Financial Group Inc., Toronto-Dominion Bank, Evercore Inc. and Cantor Fitzgerald. Shares are expected to begin trading Friday on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ETRA.

items.title: El Niño Puts India on Track for Driest Monsoon Since 2009
body: India is on course for its driest monsoon in 17 years as a strengthening El Niño curbs rainfall, threatening crop yields and raising food-price risks.

Cumulative rainfall during the June to September monsoon season is 15% below the long-term average so far, according to the India Meteorological Department. If the deficit persists, it would be the weakest monsoon since 2009, when precipitation was 18% below normal. The weather office had forecast a 10% shortfall for this season back in May.

Conditions may become favorable for a tropical cyclone in the Bay of Bengal in the last week of September, said Christian Werner, managing director of Australia-based consultancy Global Weather Climate Analytics. That could potentially bring much-needed rain to eastern and northeastern India, mitigating the deficit there, he added.
Read More: Powerful El Niño Nears Record Strength, US Forecasters Say
Still, the storm is unlikely to materially change the national picture and Werner expects the seasonal deficit to hold between 13% and 16%.

Forecasters and academics are also placing bets on India’s monsoon through a specialty prediction platform at Lancaster University in the UK, known by its acronym CRUCIAL. With less than two weeks of monsoon remaining, the platform is assigning a 68% chance that the season will end with a rainfall deficit of 10% to 20%, according to founder and planetary scientist Mark Roulston.

Adequate monsoon rains are crucial for the hundreds of millions of Indian farmers who depend on the seasonal precipitation to irrigate fields in the country, which is among the world’s biggest producers of rice, sugar and cotton. The season accounts for most of India’s annual rainfall.
Read More: A Dozen Ingredients Show India’s Mounting Food Inflation Risk

The prolonged shortfall could hurt both the current harvest and the next crop cycle, adding to the pressure on food prices that are already accelerating, with costs rising for a seventh straight month to 5.95% in August, the highest level this year. Rice, sugar cane and corn plantings are running behind last season.

When the monsoon is deficient, every 1 percentage-point shortfall in precipitation from normal levels typically raises food inflation by about 25 basis points, according to Yuvika Singhal, an economist at QuantEco.

Weaker rains and rising prices have already pushed the government to allow duty-free sugar imports to bolster supplies. The government is also selling onions at subsidized prices in some states, as part of efforts to cool rising food costs.

items.title: Vietnam Stocks See Early Foreign Flows as FTSE Upgrade Nears
body: Global funds are dipping back into Vietnamese stocks ahead of their inclusion in FTSE Russell’s emerging markets universe next week.
Foreigners have bought $54.2 million of local shares on a net basis so far this week, set for the most in six weeks. Vietnam’s reclassification by FTSE takes effect on Sept. 21.

Foreign selling in Vietnamese shares have slowed in recent months, helping the benchmark to erase losses for the year. The country in August secured a bigger-than-expected weighting in FTSE Russell’s semi-annual index review, paving the way for billions in foreign stock inflows.
“Foreign re-engagement in Vietnamese equities could build gradually as FTSE inclusion is phased in and market access improves,” said Sufianti, a Singapore-based analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence.
Passive funds that track FTSE indexes are expected to execute orders later Friday as they look to mirror the country’s weight in the index provider’s emerging-market gauge.

Global funds remain substantial sellers on an annual basis, withdrawing a net $3.5 billion of shares so far this year. That adds to the record $4.8 billion outflow in 2025, as geopolitical tensions and a rotation toward faster-growing markets weighed on demand.

items.title: Gold Extends Gain as Lower Oil, Fed Hike Temper Inflation Fears
body: Gold held a gain at the end of a volatile week as the Federal Reserve’s first interest-rate hike since 2023 and lower oil prices helped ease concerns about inflation.

Bullion was trading around $4,350 an ounce, after gaining almost 2% on Thursday to erase much of the loss from the previous three sessions. Treasury yields declined across maturities, after spiking in the wake of the Fed’s unanimous decision on Wednesday to raise rates by a quarter percentage point. That shift lifted some pressure on gold, which typically underperforms when bond yields are higher because it doesn’t pay interest.
Read More: Treasuries Gain as Oil Retreat Shores Up Confidence in Warsh Fed

Oil declined for a third day as supply disruptions in the Middle East looked set to ease, relieving energy cost pressures on inflation. Saudi Arabia has moved to restore flows along a vital pipeline within days, while some tankers have continued to traverse the contested Strait of Hormuz.
Thursday’s rebound has taken gold back above the 100-day moving average, a measure of momentum. Even so, it’s still nearly a fifth below levels before the Iran war began in late February.

Investors have been flocking to bullion in recent weeks, betting that the long-term drivers of the metal will endure. Gold-backed exchange-traded funds tracked by Bloomberg have seen inflows even as prices fell.

Still, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh’s rhetoric on inflation drove up market expectations for at least one more increase this year and up to another two in 2027, which present potential headwinds for bullion.

Spot gold rose 0.2% to $4,351.96 an ounce at 8:12 a.m. in Singapore. Silver advanced 0.4% to $65.51 an ounce, after surging 3.6% the day before. Platinum and palladium edged higher. The Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index, a gauge of the US currency, was little changed after falling 0.1% the previous session.

items.title: Citi's Korea Trading Head Says Buy Won Near 1,400 Per Dollar
body: The won’s recent weakness may be short lived as South Korea’s chip sector bolsters growth, supporting the currency’s recovery against the dollar by year-end, according to a Citigroup Inc. trader.

“There is a risk the won could fall past 1,400 per dollar in the near term,” driven by external factors such as a hawkish Federal Reserve and inflation concerns linked to higher oil prices,” Lee Sanghun, head of Korea trading, said in an interview late Wednesday. “I don’t think it will stay that weak for long, so levels around 1,400 would be a good opportunity to sell dollars and buy the won.”

After a two-month rally that made it Asia’s top-performing currency, the won declined for a fourth straight session Thursday, touching as low as 1,388.25 per dollar. A hawkish Federal Reserve is weighing on the won as US rate hikes widen the interest-rate differential with Korea, potentially denting the appeal of local assets.
The currency opened steady around 1,381.00 per dollar Friday morning.

The Fed’s move prompted traders to price in additional rate hikes, partially reversing the dollar debasement story, Lee said. Still, he maintained his year-end target of 1,330 for the won, citing strong domestic fundamentals.
While Lee expects the won to strengthen further, he said gains are unlikely to match the pace of the past two months. The currency climbed to is highest level in about two years earlier this month.
Read More: Goldman, BNP Calling for Further Gains in Surging Korean Won
External risks could make for a “bumpy road” ahead, while Korea’s massive current-account surplus doesn’t necessarily mean companies will convert all their dollar earnings into won, Lee said.

He also sees scope for the won to strengthen to the upper 1,200s in the first half of 2027 if the semiconductor cycle remains strong, chip exporters resume large-scale dollar selling and tensions in the Middle East ease.

Exporters sold dollars “too hastily in July and August,” and are probably flush with won liquidity, leaving them with “no urgency” to sell more now, Lee added, citing his observations from client meetings and business trips.

items.title: RBA Must Judge If Rates High Enough to Cool Prices, Bullock Says
body: Australia’s central bank needs to decide later this month whether its benchmark interest rate is at a level sufficient to restrain price pressures and return inflation to target, Governor Michele Bullock said.

“The Monetary Policy Board will meet in just over a week’s time. We’ll discuss our assessment of the flow of data and how the risks are unfolding,” the Reserve Bank chief said in her opening statement to a parliamentary panel on Friday.  “A key question is whether the tightening in monetary policy to date will be sufficient to bring inflation back to target in a reasonable time.”

The Australian dollar edged higher as markets interpreted the governor’s comments as slightly hawkish. Bullock is often cautious in her language to avoid being seen as pre-empting the decisions of the nine-member policy board that includes six independent directors.

The yield on three-year notes trimmed an earlier decline as traders solidified bets the RBA will hike at the September meeting. Traders priced a roughly 90% chance of a hike at the meeting, up from about 84% prior to the testimony.

The remarks are Bullock’s first significant public comments since the RBA’s August policy decision, when it held the key interest rate unchanged at 4.35% for a second straight meeting. Officials have been signaling mounting concerns that inflation has been too high for too long and are worried about additional price pressures.
“I recognise that higher interest rates are difficult for Australians with mortgages who are also facing cost-of-living pressures,” Bullock said. “But reducing inflation is essential.”

The Federal Reserve this week lifted borrowing costs for the first time since 2023 and projected further hikes to contain inflation. A number of other developed-world central banks have also either hiked or said they’re considering doing so.
Read more: Australia’s Housing Slump to Slow Economy, Assist RBA, HSBC Says
When the RBA released updated forecasts early last month, it warned that risks were skewed to the upside.
“Developments since then suggest that although growth in the Australian economy is slowing, some of these upside risks to inflation appear to be materializing,” Bullock said.
The governor highlighted that there seems to be little early prospect of a resolution to the Middle East conflict.

The US and Iran exchanged strikes on oil tankers in the Persian Gulf earlier this month as tensions have flared anew in the Strait of Hormuz. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia has come under pressure from Tehran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen. Brent crude surged back above $100 a barrel this month, fanning fears over energy-linked inflation pressures.

“Through our liaison program, we are hearing that many firms are passing on higher input costs,” Bullock said. “This was expected. But it is important that these effects remain contained and do not become embedded into price and wage setting decisions. Otherwise, inflation could prove more persistent and require a stronger policy response.”
